Creational Design Patterns

Creational patterns provide object creation mechanisms that increase flexibility and reuse of existing code.

Singleton​

Ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access to it.

Problem​

The Application needs one, and only one, instance of an object. Additionally, that object needs to be accessible from multiple parts of the application. Common examples include a database connection pool, a logger, or a configuration manager.

If multiple instances were created, it could lead to incorrect program behavior, resource overuse, or inconsistent results.

Solution​

The Singleton pattern solves this by:

  1. Hiding the constructor of the class to preventing direct instantiation.
  2. Declaring a static method (like getInstance()) that acts as a constructor. This method calls the private constructor to create an object and saves it in a static field. All following calls to this method return the cached object.

Structure​

How to Implement​

  1. Add a private static field to the class for storing the singleton instance.
  2. Declare a public static creation method for getting the singleton instance.
  3. Implement "lazy initialization" inside the static method. It should create a new object on its first call and put it into the static field.
  4. Make the constructor of the class private. The static method of the class will still be able to call the constructor, but not the other objects.
  5. Go over the client code and replace all direct calls to the singleton's constructor with calls to its static creation method.

TypeScript Example​

class Singleton {
  private static instance: Singleton;

  private constructor() {}

  public static getInstance(): Singleton {
    if (!Singleton.instance) {
      Singleton.instance = new Singleton();
    }
    return Singleton.instance;
  }

  public someBusinessLogic(): void {
    console.log('Business logic executed.');
  }
}

const s1 = Singleton.getInstance();
const s2 = Singleton.getInstance();

console.log(s1 === s2); // true

Go Example​

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "sync"
)

type singleton struct{}

var instance *singleton
var once sync.Once

func GetInstance() *singleton {
    once.Do(func() {
        instance = &singleton{}
    })
    return instance
}

func main() {
    s1 := GetInstance()
    s2 := GetInstance()

    if s1 == s2 {
        fmt.Println("Singleton works, both variables contain the same instance.")
    } else {
        fmt.Println("Singleton failed, variables contain different instances.")
    }
}

Pros and Cons​

ProsCons
✓ You can be sure that a class has only a single instance.✗ Violates the Single Responsibility Principle. The pattern solves two problems at the time.
✓ You gain a global access point to that instance.✗ The Singleton pattern can mask bad design, for instance, when the components of the program know too much about each other.
✓ The singleton object is initialized only when it's requested for the first time.✗ The pattern requires special treatment in a multithreaded environment so that multiple threads won't create a singleton object several times.
✗ It may be difficult to unit test the client code of the Singleton because many test frameworks rely on inheritance when producing mock objects.

Relations with Other Patterns​

  • Facade class is often a Singleton because a single facade object is sufficient for most application needs.
  • Flyweight would resemble Singleton if you somehow managed to reduce all shared states of the objects to just one flyweight object.
  • Abstract Factories, Builders, and Prototypes can all be implemented as Singletons.

Real-World Use Cases​

1. Database Connection Pool​

Managing a shared pool of database connections to prevent initialization overhead.

JavaScript Implementation:

class DatabasePool {
  static instance = null;
  static connections = [];

  constructor() {
    if (DatabasePool.instance) {
      return DatabasePool.instance;
    }
    DatabasePool.instance = this;
    this.maxConnections = 10;
    this.activeConnections = 0;
  }

  async getConnection() {
    if (this.activeConnections < this.maxConnections) {
      this.activeConnections++;
      // Simulate connection creation (use real DB driver in production)
      return { id: this.activeConnections, query: async (sql) => console.log(sql) };
    }
    throw new Error('Connection pool exhausted');
  }

  releaseConnection(conn) {
    this.activeConnections--;
  }
}

// Usage
const pool1 = new DatabasePool();
const pool2 = new DatabasePool();
console.log(pool1 === pool2); // true

Go Implementation:

type DBPool struct {
    maxConnections    int
    activeConnections int
    mu                sync.Mutex
}

var dbInstance *DBPool
var dbOnce sync.Once

func GetDBPool() *DBPool {
    dbOnce.Do(func() {
        dbInstance = &DBPool{
            maxConnections: 10,
        }
    })
    return dbInstance
}

func (p *DBPool) GetConnection() error {
    p.mu.Lock()
    defer p.mu.Unlock()

    if p.activeConnections < p.maxConnections {
        p.activeConnections++
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("connection pool exhausted")
}

2. Configuration Manager​

Centralized access to application settings loaded from files or environment variables.

JavaScript Implementation:

class ConfigManager {
  static instance = null;

  constructor() {
    if (ConfigManager.instance) {
      return ConfigManager.instance;
    }
    ConfigManager.instance = this;
    this.config = this.loadConfig();
  }

  loadConfig() {
    // Load from environment or config file
    return {
      apiUrl: process.env.API_URL || 'http://localhost:3000',
      dbHost: process.env.DB_HOST || 'localhost',
      maxRetries: parseInt(process.env.MAX_RETRIES) || 3,
    };
  }

  get(key) {
    return this.config[key];
  }

  set(key, value) {
    this.config[key] = value;
  }
}

// Usage
const config1 = new ConfigManager();
const config2 = new ConfigManager();
console.log(config1.get('apiUrl')); // http://localhost:3000

Go Implementation:

type Config struct {
    APIUrl     string
    DBHost     string
    MaxRetries int
}

var configInstance *Config
var configOnce sync.Once

func GetConfig() *Config {
    configOnce.Do(func() {
        configInstance = &Config{
            APIUrl:     getEnv("API_URL", "http://localhost:3000"),
            DBHost:     getEnv("DB_HOST", "localhost"),
            MaxRetries: getEnvInt("MAX_RETRIES", 3),
        }
    })
    return configInstance
}

func getEnv(key, defaultVal string) string {
    if val := os.Getenv(key); val != "" {
        return val
    }
    return defaultVal
}

3. Logger​

A single logging service instance for the entire app to maintain a consistent log stream.

JavaScript Implementation:

class Logger {
  static instance = null;

  constructor() {
    if (Logger.instance) {
      return Logger.instance;
    }
    Logger.instance = this;
    this.logs = [];
  }

  log(level, message) {
    const entry = {
      timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
      level,
      message,
    };
    this.logs.push(entry);
    console.log(`[${entry.timestamp}] ${level.toUpperCase()}: ${message}`);
  }

  info(message) {
    this.log('info', message);
  }
  warn(message) {
    this.log('warn', message);
  }
  error(message) {
    this.log('error', message);
  }

  getLogs() {
    return this.logs;
  }
}

// Usage
const logger1 = new Logger();
const logger2 = new Logger();
logger1.info('Application started');
logger2.error('An error occurred');
console.log(logger1 === logger2); // true

Go Implementation:

type Logger struct {
    logs []LogEntry
    mu   sync.Mutex
}

type LogEntry struct {
    Timestamp time.Time
    Level     string
    Message   string
}

var loggerInstance *Logger
var loggerOnce sync.Once

func GetLogger() *Logger {
    loggerOnce.Do(func() {
        loggerInstance = &Logger{
            logs: make([]LogEntry, 0),
        }
    })
    return loggerInstance
}

func (l *Logger) Log(level, message string) {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()

    entry := LogEntry{
        Timestamp: time.Now(),
        Level:     level,
        Message:   message,
    }
    l.logs = append(l.logs, entry)
    fmt.Printf("[%s] %s: %s\n", entry.Timestamp, level, message)
}

4. Cache Manager​

Managing in-memory data caching to ensure data consistency across the application.

JavaScript Implementation:

class CacheManager {
  static instance = null;

  constructor() {
    if (CacheManager.instance) {
      return CacheManager.instance;
    }
    CacheManager.instance = this;
    this.cache = new Map();
  }

  set(key, value, ttl = 3600000) {
    // Default TTL: 1 hour
    const expiry = Date.now() + ttl;
    this.cache.set(key, { value, expiry });
  }

  get(key) {
    const item = this.cache.get(key);
    if (!item) return null;

    if (Date.now() > item.expiry) {
      this.cache.delete(key);
      return null;
    }

    return item.value;
  }

  clear() {
    this.cache.clear();
  }
}

// Usage
const cache = new CacheManager();
cache.set('user:1', { name: 'John' });
console.log(cache.get('user:1')); // { name: 'John' }

Go Implementation:

type CacheItem struct {
    Value  interface{}
    Expiry time.Time
}

type CacheManager struct {
    cache map[string]CacheItem
    mu    sync.RWMutex
}

var cacheInstance *CacheManager
var cacheOnce sync.Once

func GetCache() *CacheManager {
    cacheOnce.Do(func() {
        cacheInstance = &CacheManager{
            cache: make(map[string]CacheItem),
        }
    })
    return cacheInstance
}

func (c *CacheManager) Set(key string, value interface{}, ttl time.Duration) {
    c.mu.Lock()
    defer c.mu.Unlock()

    c.cache[key] = CacheItem{
        Value:  value,
        Expiry: time.Now().Add(ttl),
    }
}

func (c *CacheManager) Get(key string) (interface{}, bool) {
    c.mu.RLock()
    defer c.mu.RUnlock()

    item, exists := c.cache[key]
    if !exists || time.Now().After(item.Expiry) {
        return nil, false
    }
    return item.Value, true
}

5. Thread Pool​

Managing a pool of worker threads to efficiently reuse resources.

JavaScript Implementation:

class WorkerPool {
  static instance = null;

  constructor(size = 4) {
    if (WorkerPool.instance) {
      return WorkerPool.instance;
    }
    WorkerPool.instance = this;
    this.workers = [];
    this.queue = [];
    this.activeWorkers = 0;
    this.maxWorkers = size;
  }

  async execute(task) {
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      if (this.activeWorkers < this.maxWorkers) {
        this.runTask(task, resolve, reject);
      } else {
        this.queue.push({ task, resolve, reject });
      }
    });
  }

  async runTask(task, resolve, reject) {
    this.activeWorkers++;
    try {
      const result = await task();
      resolve(result);
    } catch (error) {
      reject(error);
    } finally {
      this.activeWorkers--;
      if (this.queue.length > 0) {
        const next = this.queue.shift();
        this.runTask(next.task, next.resolve, next.reject);
      }
    }
  }
}

// Usage
const pool = new WorkerPool(2);
pool.execute(() => heavyComputation());

Go Implementation:

type WorkerPool struct {
    maxWorkers int
    taskQueue  chan func()
    wg         sync.WaitGroup
}

var poolInstance *WorkerPool
var poolOnce sync.Once

func GetWorkerPool(size int) *WorkerPool {
    poolOnce.Do(func() {
        poolInstance = &WorkerPool{
            maxWorkers: size,
            taskQueue:  make(chan func(), 100),
        }
        poolInstance.start()
    })
    return poolInstance
}

func (p *WorkerPool) start() {
    for i := 0; i < p.maxWorkers; i++ {
        go p.worker()
    }
}

func (p *WorkerPool) worker() {
    for task := range p.taskQueue {
        task()
        p.wg.Done()
    }
}

func (p *WorkerPool) Execute(task func()) {
    p.wg.Add(1)
    p.taskQueue <- task
}

6. Device Access​

Controlling access to hardware resources (e.g., printer spooler) to prevent conflicts.

JavaScript Implementation:

class PrinterSpooler {
  static instance = null;

  constructor() {
    if (PrinterSpooler.instance) {
      return PrinterSpooler.instance;
    }
    PrinterSpooler.instance = this;
    this.queue = [];
    this.printing = false;
  }

  async addJob(document) {
    this.queue.push(document);
    if (!this.printing) {
      await this.processQueue();
    }
  }

  async processQueue() {
    this.printing = true;
    while (this.queue.length > 0) {
      const doc = this.queue.shift();
      await this.print(doc);
    }
    this.printing = false;
  }

  async print(document) {
    console.log(`Printing: ${document.name}`);
    // Simulate printing time
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 1000));
    console.log(`Finished: ${document.name}`);
  }
}

// Usage
const spooler = new PrinterSpooler();
spooler.addJob({ name: 'Document1.pdf' });

Go Implementation:

type PrintJob struct {
    Name string
    Data []byte
}

type PrinterSpooler struct {
    queue    []PrintJob
    printing bool
    mu       sync.Mutex
}

var spoolerInstance *PrinterSpooler
var spoolerOnce sync.Once

func GetSpooler() *PrinterSpooler {
    spoolerOnce.Do(func() {
        spoolerInstance = &PrinterSpooler{
            queue: make([]PrintJob, 0),
        }
    })
    return spoolerInstance
}

func (s *PrinterSpooler) AddJob(job PrintJob) {
    s.mu.Lock()
    s.queue = append(s.queue, job)
    printing := s.printing
    s.mu.Unlock()

    if !printing {
        go s.processQueue()
    }
}

func (s *PrinterSpooler) processQueue() {
    s.mu.Lock()
    s.printing = true
    s.mu.Unlock()

    for {
        s.mu.Lock()
        if len(s.queue) == 0 {
            s.printing = false
            s.mu.Unlock()
            break
        }
        job := s.queue[0]
        s.queue = s.queue[1:]
        s.mu.Unlock()

        s.print(job)
    }
}

7. State Management​

Store (like Redux, Vuex, or Zustand) in frontend applications to manage global state.

JavaScript Implementation:

class StateStore {
  static instance = null;

  constructor() {
    if (StateStore.instance) {
      return StateStore.instance;
    }
    StateStore.instance = this;
    this.state = {};
    this.listeners = [];
  }

  getState() {
    return { ...this.state };
  }

  setState(newState) {
    this.state = { ...this.state, ...newState };
    this.notify();
  }

  subscribe(listener) {
    this.listeners.push(listener);
    return () => {
      this.listeners = this.listeners.filter((l) => l !== listener);
    };
  }

  notify() {
    this.listeners.forEach((listener) => listener(this.state));
  }
}

// Usage
const store = new StateStore();
store.subscribe((state) => console.log('State updated:', state));
store.setState({ user: { name: 'Alice' } });

Go Implementation:

type StateStore struct {
    state     map[string]interface{}
    listeners []func(map[string]interface{})
    mu        sync.RWMutex
}

var storeInstance *StateStore
var storeOnce sync.Once

func GetStore() *StateStore {
    storeOnce.Do(func() {
        storeInstance = &StateStore{
            state:     make(map[string]interface{}),
            listeners: make([]func(map[string]interface{}), 0),
        }
    })
    return storeInstance
}

func (s *StateStore) GetState() map[string]interface{} {
    s.mu.RLock()
    defer s.mu.RUnlock()

    stateCopy := make(map[string]interface{})
    for k, v := range s.state {
        stateCopy[k] = v
    }
    return stateCopy
}

func (s *StateStore) SetState(key string, value interface{}) {
    s.mu.Lock()
    s.state[key] = value
    listeners := s.listeners
    s.mu.Unlock()

    for _, listener := range listeners {
        listener(s.GetState())
    }
}

8. Feature Flags​

Singleton service to check enabled/disabled features across the codebase.

JavaScript Implementation:

class FeatureFlags {
  static instance = null;

  constructor() {
    if (FeatureFlags.instance) {
      return FeatureFlags.instance;
    }
    FeatureFlags.instance = this;
    this.flags = this.loadFlags();
  }

  loadFlags() {
    // Load from API or config
    return {
      'new-ui': true,
      'beta-features': false,
      'dark-mode': true,
      'experimental-api': false,
    };
  }

  isEnabled(flagName) {
    return this.flags[flagName] === true;
  }

  enable(flagName) {
    this.flags[flagName] = true;
  }

  disable(flagName) {
    this.flags[flagName] = false;
  }
}

// Usage
const flags = new FeatureFlags();
if (flags.isEnabled('new-ui')) {
  console.log('Rendering new UI');
}

Go Implementation:

type FeatureFlags struct {
    flags map[string]bool
    mu    sync.RWMutex
}

var flagsInstance *FeatureFlags
var flagsOnce sync.Once

func GetFeatureFlags() *FeatureFlags {
    flagsOnce.Do(func() {
        flagsInstance = &FeatureFlags{
            flags: map[string]bool{
                "new-ui":          true,
                "beta-features":   false,
                "dark-mode":       true,
                "experimental-api": false,
            },
        }
    })
    return flagsInstance
}

func (f *FeatureFlags) IsEnabled(flagName string) bool {
    f.mu.RLock()
    defer f.mu.RUnlock()
    return f.flags[flagName]
}

func (f *FeatureFlags) Enable(flagName string) {
    f.mu.Lock()
    defer f.mu.Unlock()
    f.flags[flagName] = true
}

9. Registry​

Service locator or registry pattern to store and retrieve dependencies.

JavaScript Implementation:

class ServiceRegistry {
  static instance = null;

  constructor() {
    if (ServiceRegistry.instance) {
      return ServiceRegistry.instance;
    }
    ServiceRegistry.instance = this;
    this.services = new Map();
  }

  register(name, service) {
    this.services.set(name, service);
  }

  get(name) {
    if (!this.services.has(name)) {
      throw new Error(`Service '${name}' not found`);
    }
    return this.services.get(name);
  }

  has(name) {
    return this.services.has(name);
  }
}

// Usage
const registry = new ServiceRegistry();
registry.register('database', new DatabaseService());
registry.register('logger', new Logger());

const db = registry.get('database');

Go Implementation:

type ServiceRegistry struct {
    services map[string]interface{}
    mu       sync.RWMutex
}

var registryInstance *ServiceRegistry
var registryOnce sync.Once

func GetRegistry() *ServiceRegistry {
    registryOnce.Do(func() {
        registryInstance = &ServiceRegistry{
            services: make(map[string]interface{}),
        }
    })
    return registryInstance
}

func (r *ServiceRegistry) Register(name string, service interface{}) {
    r.mu.Lock()
    defer r.mu.Unlock()
    r.services[name] = service
}

func (r *ServiceRegistry) Get(name string) (interface{}, error) {
    r.mu.RLock()
    defer r.mu.RUnlock()

    service, exists := r.services[name]
    if !exists {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("service '%s' not found", name)
    }
    return service, nil
}

10. File System Interface​

Abstracting file system operations to a single point of entry.

JavaScript Implementation:

const fs = require('fs').promises;
const path = require('path');

class FileSystemManager {
  static instance = null;

  constructor() {
    if (FileSystemManager.instance) {
      return FileSystemManager.instance;
    }
    FileSystemManager.instance = this;
    this.cache = new Map();
  }

  async readFile(filePath) {
    if (this.cache.has(filePath)) {
      return this.cache.get(filePath);
    }

    const content = await fs.readFile(filePath, 'utf-8');
    this.cache.set(filePath, content);
    return content;
  }

  async writeFile(filePath, content) {
    await fs.writeFile(filePath, content, 'utf-8');
    this.cache.set(filePath, content);
  }

  clearCache() {
    this.cache.clear();
  }
}

// Usage
const fsManager = new FileSystemManager();
const content = await fsManager.readFile('/path/to/file.txt');

Go Implementation:

type FileSystemManager struct {
    cache map[string]string
    mu    sync.RWMutex
}

var fsInstance *FileSystemManager
var fsOnce sync.Once

func GetFileSystemManager() *FileSystemManager {
    fsOnce.Do(func() {
        fsInstance = &FileSystemManager{
            cache: make(map[string]string),
        }
    })
    return fsInstance
}

func (f *FileSystemManager) ReadFile(filePath string) (string, error) {
    f.mu.RLock()
    if content, exists := f.cache[filePath]; exists {
        f.mu.RUnlock()
        return content, nil
    }
    f.mu.RUnlock()

    data, err := os.ReadFile(filePath)
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }

    content := string(data)
    f.mu.Lock()
    f.cache[filePath] = content
    f.mu.Unlock()

    return content, nil
}

func (f *FileSystemManager) WriteFile(filePath, content string) error {
    err := os.WriteFile(filePath, []byte(content), 0644)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }

    f.mu.Lock()
    f.cache[filePath] = content
    f.mu.Unlock()

    return nil
}

Factory Method​

Defines an interface for creating an object, but let subclasses decide which class to instantiate.

Problem​

Imagine that you’re creating a logistics management application. The first version of your app can only handle transportation by trucks, so the bulk of your code lives inside the Truck class.

After a while, your app becomes pretty popular. Each day you receive dozens of requests from sea transportation companies to incorporate sea logistics into the app.

Great news, right? But how about the code? At present, most of your code is coupled to the Truck class. Adding Ships into the app would require making changes to the entire codebase. Moreover, if later you decide to add another type of transportation to the app, you will probably need to make all of these changes again.

Solution​

The Factory Method pattern suggests that you replace direct object construction calls (using the new operator) with calls to a special factory method. The objects are still created via the new operator, but it's being called from within the factory method. Objects returned by a factory method are often referred to as products.

Structure​

How to Implement​

  1. Make all products follow the same interface.
  2. Add an empty factory method inside the creator class. The return type of the method should match the common product interface.
  3. In the creator's code, find all references to product constructors. One by one, replace them with calls to the factory method, while extracting the product creation code into the factory method.
  4. Create a set of creator subclasses for each type of product listed in the factory method. Override the factory method in the subclasses and extract the appropriate bits of construction code from the base method.

TypeScript Example​

interface Product {
  operation(): string;
}

class ConcreteProductA implements Product {
  public operation(): string {
    return '{Result of the ConcreteProductA}';
  }
}

class ConcreteProductB implements Product {
  public operation(): string {
    return '{Result of the ConcreteProductB}';
  }
}

abstract class Creator {
  public abstract factoryMethod(): Product;

  public someOperation(): string {
    const product = this.factoryMethod();
    return `Creator: The same creator's code has just worked with ${product.operation()}`;
  }
}

class ConcreteCreatorA extends Creator {
  public factoryMethod(): Product {
    return new ConcreteProductA();
  }
}

class ConcreteCreatorB extends Creator {
  public factoryMethod(): Product {
    return new ConcreteProductB();
  }
}

Go Example​

package main

import "fmt"

type Product interface {
    Use() string
}

type ConcreteProductA struct{}

func (p *ConcreteProductA) Use() string {
    return "Result of ConcreteProductA"
}

type ConcreteProductB struct{}

func (p *ConcreteProductB) Use() string {
    return "Result of ConcreteProductB"
}

type Creator interface {
    CreateProduct() Product
}

type ConcreteCreatorA struct{}

func (c *ConcreteCreatorA) CreateProduct() Product {
    return &ConcreteProductA{}
}

type ConcreteCreatorB struct{}

func (c *ConcreteCreatorB) CreateProduct() Product {
    return &ConcreteProductB{}
}

func main() {
    creators := []Creator{&ConcreteCreatorA{}, &ConcreteCreatorB{}}
    for _, creator := range creators {
        product := creator.CreateProduct()
        fmt.Printf("Created: %s\n", product.Use())
    }
}

Pros and Cons​

ProsCons
✓ You avoid tight coupling between the creator and the concrete products.✗ The code may become more complicated since you need to introduce a lot of new subclasses to implement the pattern.
✓ Single Responsibility Principle. You can move the product creation code into one place in the program, making the code easier to support.
✓ Open/Closed Principle. You can introduce new types of products into the program without breaking existing client code.

Relations with Other Patterns​

  • Abstract Factory classes are often implemented with a set of Factory Methods.
  • Template Method: Factory Method is a specialization of Template Method.
  • Prototypes: Prototype isn't based on inheritance, so it doesn't have the downsides of Factory Method.

Real-World Use Cases​

1. Cross-Platform UI Elements​

Creating native-looking buttons or dialogs for different OSs (Windows, Mac, Linux) dynamically.

JavaScript Implementation:

// Product Interface
class Button {
  render() {
    throw new Error('Method not implemented');
  }
}

// Concrete Products
class WindowsButton extends Button {
  render() {
    return '<button class="windows-style">Click me</button>';
  }
}

class MacButton extends Button {
  render() {
    return '<button class="mac-style">Click me</button>';
  }
}

class LinuxButton extends Button {
  render() {
    return '<button class="linux-style">Click me</button>';
  }
}

// Factory
class UIFactory {
  createButton() {
    throw new Error('Factory method not implemented');
  }
}

class WindowsFactory extends UIFactory {
  createButton() {
    return new WindowsButton();
  }
}

class MacFactory extends UIFactory {
  createButton() {
    return new MacButton();
  }
}

// Usage
const platform = process.platform;
let factory;
if (platform === 'win32') factory = new WindowsFactory();
else if (platform === 'darwin') factory = new MacFactory();
else factory = new LinuxFactory();

const button = factory.createButton();
console.log(button.render());

Go Implementation:

type Button interface {
    Render() string
}

type WindowsButton struct{}
func (b *WindowsButton) Render() string {
    return "<button class='windows-style'>Click me</button>"
}

type MacButton struct{}
func (b *MacButton) Render() string {
    return "<button class='mac-style'>Click me</button>"
}

type UIFactory interface {
    CreateButton() Button
}

type WindowsFactory struct{}
func (f *WindowsFactory) CreateButton() Button {
    return &WindowsButton{}
}

type MacFactory struct{}
func (f *MacFactory) CreateButton() Button {
    return &MacButton{}
}

// Usage
func GetFactory(platform string) UIFactory {
    switch platform {
    case "windows":
        return &WindowsFactory{}
    case "mac":
        return &MacFactory{}
    default:
        return &WindowsFactory{}
    }
}

2. Payment Gateway Integration​

Creating specific handlers for Stripe, PayPal, or Square based on user selection.

JavaScript Implementation:

class PaymentGateway {
  async processPayment(amount, currency) {
    throw new Error('Method not implemented');
  }
}

class StripeGateway extends PaymentGateway {
  async processPayment(amount, currency) {
    console.log(`Processing $${amount} ${currency} via Stripe`);
    // Stripe API integration
    return { success: true, transactionId: 'stripe_' + Date.now() };
  }
}

class PayPalGateway extends PaymentGateway {
  async processPayment(amount, currency) {
    console.log(`Processing $${amount} ${currency} via PayPal`);
    // PayPal API integration
    return { success: true, transactionId: 'paypal_' + Date.now() };
  }
}

class SquareGateway extends PaymentGateway {
  async processPayment(amount, currency) {
    console.log(`Processing $${amount} ${currency} via Square`);
    // Square API integration
    return { success: true, transactionId: 'square_' + Date.now() };
  }
}

class PaymentFactory {
  static createGateway(type) {
    switch (type) {
      case 'stripe':
        return new StripeGateway();
      case 'paypal':
        return new PayPalGateway();
      case 'square':
        return new SquareGateway();
      default:
        throw new Error(`Unknown payment gateway: ${type}`);
    }
  }
}

// Usage
const gateway = PaymentFactory.createGateway('stripe');
await gateway.processPayment(100, 'USD');

Go Implementation:

type PaymentGateway interface {
    ProcessPayment(amount float64, currency string) (map[string]interface{}, error)
}

type StripeGateway struct{}
func (g *StripeGateway) ProcessPayment(amount float64, currency string) (map[string]interface{}, error) {
    fmt.Printf("Processing $%.2f %s via Stripe\n", amount, currency)
    return map[string]interface{}{
        "success":       true,
        "transactionId": "stripe_" + time.Now().String(),
    }, nil
}

type PayPalGateway struct{}
func (g *PayPalGateway) ProcessPayment(amount float64, currency string) (map[string]interface{}, error) {
    fmt.Printf("Processing $%.2f %s via PayPal\n", amount, currency)
    return map[string]interface{}{
        "success":       true,
        "transactionId": "paypal_" + time.Now().String(),
    }, nil
}

func CreatePaymentGateway(gatewayType string) (PaymentGateway, error) {
    switch gatewayType {
    case "stripe":
        return &StripeGateway{}, nil
    case "paypal":
        return &PayPalGateway{}, nil
    default:
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("unknown payment gateway: %s", gatewayType)
    }
}

3. Document Export​

Generating PDF, CSV, or Excel reports from the same data source.

JavaScript Implementation:

class DocumentExporter {
  export(data) {
    throw new Error('Method not implemented');
  }
}

class PDFExporter extends DocumentExporter {
  export(data) {
    console.log('Exporting to PDF...');
    // Use library like pdfkit
    return {
      format: 'pdf',
      content: `PDF content from ${data.length} records`,
      filename: 'report.pdf',
    };
  }
}

class CSVExporter extends DocumentExporter {
  export(data) {
    console.log('Exporting to CSV...');
    const headers = Object.keys(data[0]).join(',');
    const rows = data.map((row) => Object.values(row).join(','));
    return {
      format: 'csv',
      content: [headers, ...rows].join('\n'),
      filename: 'report.csv',
    };
  }
}

class ExcelExporter extends DocumentExporter {
  export(data) {
    console.log('Exporting to Excel...');
    // Use library like exceljs
    return {
      format: 'xlsx',
      content: `Excel workbook with ${data.length} rows`,
      filename: 'report.xlsx',
    };
  }
}

class ExporterFactory {
  static createExporter(format) {
    switch (format.toLowerCase()) {
      case 'pdf':
        return new PDFExporter();
      case 'csv':
        return new CSVExporter();
      case 'excel':
        return new ExcelExporter();
      default:
        throw new Error(`Unsupported format: ${format}`);
    }
  }
}

// Usage
const data = [
  { name: 'John', age: 30 },
  { name: 'Jane', age: 25 },
];
const exporter = ExporterFactory.createExporter('csv');
const result = exporter.export(data);

Go Implementation:

type DocumentExporter interface {
    Export(data []map[string]interface{}) (map[string]string, error)
}

type PDFExporter struct{}
func (e *PDFExporter) Export(data []map[string]interface{}) (map[string]string, error) {
    fmt.Println("Exporting to PDF...")
    return map[string]string{
        "format":   "pdf",
        "content":  fmt.Sprintf("PDF content from %d records", len(data)),
        "filename": "report.pdf",
    }, nil
}

type CSVExporter struct{}
func (e *CSVExporter) Export(data []map[string]interface{}) (map[string]string, error) {
    fmt.Println("Exporting to CSV...")
    // CSV generation logic
    return map[string]string{
        "format":   "csv",
        "filename": "report.csv",
    }, nil
}

func CreateExporter(format string) (DocumentExporter, error) {
    switch strings.ToLower(format) {
    case "pdf":
        return &PDFExporter{}, nil
    case "csv":
        return &CSVExporter{}, nil
    default:
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("unsupported format: %s", format)
    }
}

5. Database Connectors​

Creating specific connection objects for MySQL, PostgreSQL, or SQLite based on configuration.

JavaScript Implementation:

class DatabaseConnector {
  async connect() {
    throw new Error('Method not implemented');
  }

  async query(sql) {
    throw new Error('Method not implemented');
  }
}

class MySQLConnector extends DatabaseConnector {
  constructor(config) {
    super();
    this.config = config;
  }

  async connect() {
    console.log('Connecting to MySQL...');
    // Use mysql2 library
    return { connected: true, type: 'mysql' };
  }

  async query(sql) {
    console.log(`MySQL Query: ${sql}`);
    return [];
  }
}

class PostgreSQLConnector extends DatabaseConnector {
  constructor(config) {
    super();
    this.config = config;
  }

  async connect() {
    console.log('Connecting to PostgreSQL...');
    // Use pg library
    return { connected: true, type: 'postgresql' };
  }

  async query(sql) {
    console.log(`PostgreSQL Query: ${sql}`);
    return [];
  }
}

class SQLiteConnector extends DatabaseConnector {
  constructor(config) {
    super();
    this.config = config;
  }

  async connect() {
    console.log('Connecting to SQLite...');
    // Use sqlite3 library
    return { connected: true, type: 'sqlite' };
  }

  async query(sql) {
    console.log(`SQLite Query: ${sql}`);
    return [];
  }
}

class DatabaseFactory {
  static createConnector(type, config) {
    switch (type) {
      case 'mysql':
        return new MySQLConnector(config);
      case 'postgresql':
        return new PostgreSQLConnector(config);
      case 'sqlite':
        return new SQLiteConnector(config);
      default:
        throw new Error(`Unknown database: ${type}`);
    }
  }
}

// Usage
const db = DatabaseFactory.createConnector('mysql', {
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'root',
  password: 'password',
});
await db.connect();

Go Implementation:

type DatabaseConnector interface {
    Connect() error
    Query(sql string) ([]map[string]interface{}, error)
}

type MySQLConnector struct {
    config map[string]string
}

func (c *MySQLConnector) Connect() error {
    fmt.Println("Connecting to MySQL...")
    return nil
}

func (c *MySQLConnector) Query(sql string) ([]map[string]interface{}, error) {
    fmt.Printf("MySQL Query: %s\n", sql)
    return []map[string]interface{}{}, nil
}

type PostgreSQLConnector struct {
    config map[string]string
}

func (c *PostgreSQLConnector) Connect() error {
    fmt.Println("Connecting to PostgreSQL...")
    return nil
}

func (c *PostgreSQLConnector) Query(sql string) ([]map[string]interface{}, error) {
    fmt.Printf("PostgreSQL Query: %s\n", sql)
    return []map[string]interface{}{}, nil
}

func CreateDatabaseConnector(dbType string, config map[string]string) (DatabaseConnector, error) {
    switch dbType {
    case "mysql":
        return &MySQLConnector{config: config}, nil
    case "postgresql":
        return &PostgreSQLConnector{config: config}, nil
    default:
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("unknown database: %s", dbType)
    }
}

6. Loggers​

Creating File, Console, or Remote loggers based on the environment (dev vs. prod).

JavaScript Implementation:

class Logger {
  log(level, message) {
    throw new Error('Method not implemented');
  }
}

class ConsoleLogger extends Logger {
  log(level, message) {
    const timestamp = new Date().toISOString();
    console.log(`[${timestamp}] [${level.toUpperCase()}] ${message}`);
  }
}

class FileLogger extends Logger {
  constructor(filename) {
    super();
    this.filename = filename;
  }

  log(level, message) {
    const timestamp = new Date().toISOString();
    const logEntry = `[${timestamp}] [${level.toUpperCase()}] ${message}\n`;
    // In real app, use fs.appendFile
    console.log(`Writing to ${this.filename}: ${logEntry.trim()}`);
  }
}

class RemoteLogger extends Logger {
  constructor(endpoint) {
    super();
    this.endpoint = endpoint;
  }

  async log(level, message) {
    const payload = {
      timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
      level,
      message,
    };
    console.log(`Sending to ${this.endpoint}:`, payload);
    // In real app, use fetch or axios
  }
}

class LoggerFactory {
  static createLogger(env) {
    switch (env) {
      case 'development':
        return new ConsoleLogger();
      case 'production':
        return new FileLogger('/var/log/app.log');
      case 'cloud':
        return new RemoteLogger('https://logs.example.com/api');
      default:
        return new ConsoleLogger();
    }
  }
}

// Usage
const logger = LoggerFactory.createLogger(process.env.NODE_ENV);
logger.log('info', 'Application started');

Go Implementation:

type Logger interface {
    Log(level, message string)
}

type ConsoleLogger struct{}

func (l *ConsoleLogger) Log(level, message string) {
    timestamp := time.Now().Format(time.RFC3339)
    fmt.Printf("[%s] [%s] %s\n", timestamp, strings.ToUpper(level), message)
}

type FileLogger struct {
    filename string
}

func (l *FileLogger) Log(level, message string) {
    timestamp := time.Now().Format(time.RFC3339)
    logEntry := fmt.Sprintf("[%s] [%s] %s\n", timestamp, strings.ToUpper(level), message)
    // In real app, append to file
    fmt.Printf("Writing to %s: %s", l.filename, logEntry)
}

type RemoteLogger struct {
    endpoint string
}

func (l *RemoteLogger) Log(level, message string) {
    fmt.Printf("Sending to %s: [%s] %s\n", l.endpoint, level, message)
    // In real app, make HTTP request
}

func CreateLogger(env string) Logger {
    switch env {
    case "development":
        return &ConsoleLogger{}
    case "production":
        return &FileLogger{filename: "/var/log/app.log"}
    case "cloud":
        return &RemoteLogger{endpoint: "https://logs.example.com/api"}
    default:
        return &ConsoleLogger{}
    }
}

7. Parsers​

Creating JSON, XML, or YAML parsers based on file extensions.

JavaScript Implementation:

class Parser {
  parse(content) {
    throw new Error('Method not implemented');
  }
}

class JSONParser extends Parser {
  parse(content) {
    try {
      return JSON.parse(content);
    } catch (error) {
      throw new Error(`JSON parsing error: ${error.message}`);
    }
  }
}

class XMLParser extends Parser {
  parse(content) {
    console.log('Parsing XML...');
    // Use xml2js or similar library
    return { xml: 'parsed content' };
  }
}

class YAMLParser extends Parser {
  parse(content) {
    console.log('Parsing YAML...');
    // Use js-yaml library
    return { yaml: 'parsed content' };
  }
}

class ParserFactory {
  static createParser(fileExtension) {
    switch (fileExtension.toLowerCase()) {
      case '.json':
        return new JSONParser();
      case '.xml':
        return new XMLParser();
      case '.yaml':
      case '.yml':
        return new YAMLParser();
      default:
        throw new Error(`No parser for extension: ${fileExtension}`);
    }
  }

  static parseFile(filename, content) {
    const ext = filename.substring(filename.lastIndexOf('.'));
    const parser = this.createParser(ext);
    return parser.parse(content);
  }
}

// Usage
const data = ParserFactory.parseFile('config.json', '{"key": "value"}');

Go Implementation:

type Parser interface {
    Parse(content string) (map[string]interface{}, error)
}

type JSONParser struct{}

func (p *JSONParser) Parse(content string) (map[string]interface{}, error) {
    var result map[string]interface{}
    err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(content), &result)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("JSON parsing error: %v", err)
    }
    return result, nil
}

type XMLParser struct{}

func (p *XMLParser) Parse(content string) (map[string]interface{}, error) {
    fmt.Println("Parsing XML...")
    // Use encoding/xml package
    return map[string]interface{}{"xml": "parsed content"}, nil
}

type YAMLParser struct{}

func (p *YAMLParser) Parse(content string) (map[string]interface{}, error) {
    fmt.Println("Parsing YAML...")
    // Use gopkg.in/yaml.v2
    return map[string]interface{}{"yaml": "parsed content"}, nil
}

func CreateParser(fileExtension string) (Parser, error) {
    switch strings.ToLower(fileExtension) {
    case ".json":
        return &JSONParser{}, nil
    case ".xml":
        return &XMLParser{}, nil
    case ".yaml", ".yml":
        return &YAMLParser{}, nil
    default:
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("no parser for extension: %s", fileExtension)
    }
}

8. Routing Algorithms​

Creating different navigation strategies (Fastest, Shortest, Scenic) based on user choice.

JavaScript Implementation:

class RouteStrategy {
  calculateRoute(start, end) {
    throw new Error('Method not implemented');
  }
}

class FastestRoute extends RouteStrategy {
  calculateRoute(start, end) {
    console.log(`Calculating fastest route from ${start} to ${end}`);
    return {
      strategy: 'fastest',
      distance: 50,
      duration: 30,
      route: ['Highway A', 'Highway B'],
    };
  }
}

class ShortestRoute extends RouteStrategy {
  calculateRoute(start, end) {
    console.log(`Calculating shortest route from ${start} to ${end}`);
    return {
      strategy: 'shortest',
      distance: 40,
      duration: 45,
      route: ['Main St', 'Oak Ave'],
    };
  }
}

class ScenicRoute extends RouteStrategy {
  calculateRoute(start, end) {
    console.log(`Calculating scenic route from ${start} to ${end}`);
    return {
      strategy: 'scenic',
      distance: 60,
      duration: 60,
      route: ['Coastal Road', 'Mountain Pass'],
    };
  }
}

class RouteFactory {
  static createRoute(preference) {
    switch (preference) {
      case 'fastest':
        return new FastestRoute();
      case 'shortest':
        return new ShortestRoute();
      case 'scenic':
        return new ScenicRoute();
      default:
        return new FastestRoute();
    }
  }
}

// Usage
const route = RouteFactory.createRoute('scenic');
const result = route.calculateRoute('NYC', 'Boston');

Go Implementation:

type RouteStrategy interface {
    CalculateRoute(start, end string) map[string]interface{}
}

type FastestRoute struct{}

func (r *FastestRoute) CalculateRoute(start, end string) map[string]interface{} {
    fmt.Printf("Calculating fastest route from %s to %s\n", start, end)
    return map[string]interface{}{
        "strategy": "fastest",
        "distance": 50,
        "duration": 30,
        "route":    []string{"Highway A", "Highway B"},
    }
}

type ShortestRoute struct{}

func (r *ShortestRoute) CalculateRoute(start, end string) map[string]interface{} {
    fmt.Printf("Calculating shortest route from %s to %s\n", start, end)
    return map[string]interface{}{
        "strategy": "shortest",
        "distance": 40,
        "duration": 45,
        "route":    []string{"Main St", "Oak Ave"},
    }
}

func CreateRouteStrategy(preference string) RouteStrategy {
    switch preference {
    case "fastest":
        return &FastestRoute{}
    case "shortest":
        return &ShortestRoute{}
    default:
        return &FastestRoute{}
    }
}

9. Authentication Providers​

Creating OAuth, JWT, or Session auth handlers based on the requested method.

JavaScript Implementation:

class AuthProvider {
  async authenticate(credentials) {
    throw new Error('Method not implemented');
  }

  async validate(token) {
    throw new Error('Method not implemented');
  }
}

class OAuthProvider extends AuthProvider {
  async authenticate(credentials) {
    console.log('Authenticating via OAuth...');
    // OAuth flow implementation
    return {
      method: 'oauth',
      token: 'oauth_token_' + Date.now(),
      expiresIn: 3600,
    };
  }

  async validate(token) {
    console.log('Validating OAuth token...');
    return token.startsWith('oauth_token_');
  }
}

class JWTProvider extends AuthProvider {
  async authenticate(credentials) {
    console.log('Authenticating via JWT...');
    // JWT generation
    return {
      method: 'jwt',
      token: 'jwt_token_' + Date.now(),
      expiresIn: 3600,
    };
  }

  async validate(token) {
    console.log('Validating JWT token...');
    // JWT verification
    return token.startsWith('jwt_token_');
  }
}

class SessionProvider extends AuthProvider {
  constructor() {
    super();
    this.sessions = new Map();
  }

  async authenticate(credentials) {
    console.log('Creating session...');
    const sessionId = 'session_' + Date.now();
    this.sessions.set(sessionId, credentials);
    return {
      method: 'session',
      sessionId,
      expiresIn: 3600,
    };
  }

  async validate(sessionId) {
    return this.sessions.has(sessionId);
  }
}

class AuthFactory {
  static createProvider(method) {
    switch (method) {
      case 'oauth':
        return new OAuthProvider();
      case 'jwt':
        return new JWTProvider();
      case 'session':
        return new SessionProvider();
      default:
        throw new Error(`Unknown auth method: ${method}`);
    }
  }
}

// Usage
const auth = AuthFactory.createProvider('jwt');
const result = await auth.authenticate({ username: 'user', password: 'pass' });

Go Implementation:

type AuthProvider interface {
    Authenticate(credentials map[string]string) (map[string]interface{}, error)
    Validate(token string) (bool, error)
}

type OAuthProvider struct{}

func (p *OAuthProvider) Authenticate(credentials map[string]string) (map[string]interface{}, error) {
    fmt.Println("Authenticating via OAuth...")
    return map[string]interface{}{
        "method":    "oauth",
        "token":     "oauth_token_" + time.Now().String(),
        "expiresIn": 3600,
    }, nil
}

func (p *OAuthProvider) Validate(token string) (bool, error) {
    fmt.Println("Validating OAuth token...")
    return strings.HasPrefix(token, "oauth_token_"), nil
}

type JWTProvider struct{}

func (p *JWTProvider) Authenticate(credentials map[string]string) (map[string]interface{}, error) {
    fmt.Println("Authenticating via JWT...")
    return map[string]interface{}{
        "method":    "jwt",
        "token":     "jwt_token_" + time.Now().String(),
        "expiresIn": 3600,
    }, nil
}

func (p *JWTProvider) Validate(token string) (bool, error) {
    return strings.HasPrefix(token, "jwt_token_"), nil
}

func CreateAuthProvider(method string) (AuthProvider, error) {
    switch method {
    case "oauth":
        return &OAuthProvider{}, nil
    case "jwt":
        return &JWTProvider{}, nil
    default:
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("unknown auth method: %s", method)
    }
}

10. Storage Backends​

Creating S3, Local, or GCS storage interfaces based on deployment config.

JavaScript Implementation:

class StorageBackend {
  async upload(key, data) {
    throw new Error('Method not implemented');
  }

  async download(key) {
    throw new Error('Method not implemented');
  }

  async delete(key) {
    throw new Error('Method not implemented');
  }
}

class S3Storage extends StorageBackend {
  constructor(config) {
    super();
    this.bucket = config.bucket;
  }

  async upload(key, data) {
    console.log(`Uploading to S3: ${this.bucket}/${key}`);
    // AWS SDK S3 upload
    return { url: `https://${this.bucket}.s3.amazonaws.com/${key}` };
  }

  async download(key) {
    console.log(`Downloading from S3: ${this.bucket}/${key}`);
    // AWS SDK S3 download
    return 'file data';
  }

  async delete(key) {
    console.log(`Deleting from S3: ${this.bucket}/${key}`);
    return true;
  }
}

class LocalStorage extends StorageBackend {
  constructor(config) {
    super();
    this.basePath = config.basePath;
  }

  async upload(key, data) {
    const path = `${this.basePath}/${key}`;
    console.log(`Saving locally: ${path}`);
    // fs.writeFile implementation
    return { path };
  }

  async download(key) {
    const path = `${this.basePath}/${key}`;
    console.log(`Reading locally: ${path}`);
    // fs.readFile implementation
    return 'file data';
  }

  async delete(key) {
    const path = `${this.basePath}/${key}`;
    console.log(`Deleting locally: ${path}`);
    // fs.unlink implementation
    return true;
  }
}

class GCSStorage extends StorageBackend {
  constructor(config) {
    super();
    this.bucket = config.bucket;
  }

  async upload(key, data) {
    console.log(`Uploading to GCS: ${this.bucket}/${key}`);
    // Google Cloud Storage upload
    return { url: `https://storage.googleapis.com/${this.bucket}/${key}` };
  }

  async download(key) {
    console.log(`Downloading from GCS: ${this.bucket}/${key}`);
    return 'file data';
  }

  async delete(key) {
    console.log(`Deleting from GCS: ${this.bucket}/${key}`);
    return true;
  }
}

class StorageFactory {
  static createStorage(type, config) {
    switch (type) {
      case 's3':
        return new S3Storage(config);
      case 'local':
        return new LocalStorage(config);
      case 'gcs':
        return new GCSStorage(config);
      default:
        throw new Error(`Unknown storage type: ${type}`);
    }
  }
}

// Usage
const storage = StorageFactory.createStorage('s3', {
  bucket: 'my-app-bucket',
});
await storage.upload('document.pdf', fileData);

Go Implementation:

type StorageBackend interface {
    Upload(key string, data []byte) (map[string]string, error)
    Download(key string) ([]byte, error)
    Delete(key string) error
}

type S3Storage struct {
    bucket string
}

func (s *S3Storage) Upload(key string, data []byte) (map[string]string, error) {
    fmt.Printf("Uploading to S3: %s/%s\n", s.bucket, key)
    return map[string]string{
        "url": fmt.Sprintf("https://%s.s3.amazonaws.com/%s", s.bucket, key),
    }, nil
}

func (s *S3Storage) Download(key string) ([]byte, error) {
    fmt.Printf("Downloading from S3: %s/%s\n", s.bucket, key)
    return []byte("file data"), nil
}

func (s *S3Storage) Delete(key string) error {
    fmt.Printf("Deleting from S3: %s/%s\n", s.bucket, key)
    return nil
}

type LocalStorage struct {
    basePath string
}

func (s *LocalStorage) Upload(key string, data []byte) (map[string]string, error) {
    path := fmt.Sprintf("%s/%s", s.basePath, key)
    fmt.Printf("Saving locally: %s\n", path)
    return map[string]string{"path": path}, nil
}

func (s *LocalStorage) Download(key string) ([]byte, error) {
    path := fmt.Sprintf("%s/%s", s.basePath, key)
    fmt.Printf("Reading locally: %s\n", path)
    return []byte("file data"), nil
}

func (s *LocalStorage) Delete(key string) error {
    path := fmt.Sprintf("%s/%s", s.basePath, key)
    fmt.Printf("Deleting locally: %s\n", path)
    return nil
}

func CreateStorage(storageType string, config map[string]string) (StorageBackend, error) {
    switch storageType {
    case "s3":
        return &S3Storage{bucket: config["bucket"]}, nil
    case "local":
        return &LocalStorage{basePath: config["basePath"]}, nil
    default:
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("unknown storage type: %s", storageType)
    }
}

Abstract Factory​

Lets you produce families of related objects without specifying their concrete classes.

Problem​

Imagine that you're creating a furniture shop simulator. Your code consists of classes that represent:

  1. A family of related products, say: Chair + Sofa + CoffeeTable.
  2. Several variants of this family. For example, products Chair + Sofa + CoffeeTable are available in these variants: Modern, Victorian, ArtDeco.

You need a way to create individual furniture objects so that they match other objects of the same family. Customers get quite mad when they receive non-matching furniture. Also, you don't want to change existing code when adding new products or families of products.

Solution​

The Abstract Factory pattern suggests explicitly declaring interfaces for each distinct product of the product family (e.g., chair, sofa or coffee table). Then you can make all variants of products follow those interfaces. For example, all chair variants can implement the Chair interface; all coffee table variants can implement the CoffeeTable interface, and so on.

The next step is to declare the Abstract Factory—an interface with a list of creation methods for all products that are part of the product family (for example, createChair, createSofa and createCoffeeTable). These methods must return abstract product types represented by the interfaces we extracted previously: Chair, Sofa, CoffeeTable and so on.

Structure​

How to Implement​

  1. Map out a matrix of distinct product types versus variants of these products.
  2. Declare abstract product interfaces for all product types. Then make all concrete product classes implement these interfaces.
  3. Declare the abstract factory interface with a set of creation methods for all abstract products.
  4. Implement a set of concrete factory classes, one for each product variant.
  5. Create factory initialization code somewhere in the app. It should instantiate one of the concrete factory classes, usually depending on the application configuration or the current environment. Pass this factory object to all classes that construct products.
  6. Scan through the code and find all direct calls to product constructors. Replace them with calls to the appropriate creation method on the factory object.

TypeScript Example​

interface AbstractFactory {
  createProductA(): AbstractProductA;
  createProductB(): AbstractProductB;
}

class ConcreteFactory1 implements AbstractFactory {
  public createProductA(): AbstractProductA {
    return new ConcreteProductA1();
  }

  public createProductB(): AbstractProductB {
    return new ConcreteProductB1();
  }
}

class ConcreteFactory2 implements AbstractFactory {
  public createProductA(): AbstractProductA {
    return new ConcreteProductA2();
  }

  public createProductB(): AbstractProductB {
    return new ConcreteProductB2();
  }
}

interface AbstractProductA {
  usefulFunctionA(): string;
}

class ConcreteProductA1 implements AbstractProductA {
  public usefulFunctionA(): string {
    return 'The result of the product A1.';
  }
}

class ConcreteProductA2 implements AbstractProductA {
  public usefulFunctionA(): string {
    return 'The result of the product A2.';
  }
}

interface AbstractProductB {
  usefulFunctionB(): string;
  anotherUsefulFunctionB(collaborator: AbstractProductA): string;
}

class ConcreteProductB1 implements AbstractProductB {
  public usefulFunctionB(): string {
    return 'The result of the product B1.';
  }

  public anotherUsefulFunctionB(collaborator: AbstractProductA): string {
    const result = collaborator.usefulFunctionA();
    return `The result of the B1 collaborating with the (${result})`;
  }
}

class ConcreteProductB2 implements AbstractProductB {
  public usefulFunctionB(): string {
    return 'The result of the product B2.';
  }

  public anotherUsefulFunctionB(collaborator: AbstractProductA): string {
    const result = collaborator.usefulFunctionA();
    return `The result of the B2 collaborating with the (${result})`;
  }
}

Pros and Cons​

ProsCons
✓ You can be sure that the products you’re getting from a factory are compatible with each other.✗ The code may become more complicated than it should be, since a lot of new interfaces and classes are introduced along with the pattern.
✓ You avoid tight coupling between concrete products and client code.
✓ Single Responsibility Principle. You can extract the product creation code into one place, making the code easier to support.
✓ Open/Closed Principle. You can introduce new variants of products without breaking existing client code.

Relations with Other Patterns​

  • Many designs start by using Factory Method (less complicated and more customizable via subclasses) and evolve toward Abstract Factory, Prototype, or Builder (more flexible, but more complicated).
  • Builder focuses on constructing complex objects step by step. Abstract Factory specializes in creating families of related objects. Abstract Factory returns the product immediately, whereas Builder lets you run some additional construction steps before fetching the product.
  • Abstract Factory classes are often based on a set of Factory Methods, but you can also use Prototype to compose the methods on these classes.
  • Abstract Factory can serve as an alternative to Facade when you only want to hide the way the subsystem objects are created from the client code.

Real-World Use Cases​

  1. Cross-Platform GUI Libraries: Creating families of components (Buttons, Checkboxes, Windows) for Windows, macOS, or Linux.
  2. Database Access Layers: Creating families of connection, command, and parameter objects for converting between SQL flavors (MySQL, PostgreSQL).
  3. Theming Systems: Creating families of UI elements (Typography, Colors, Spacing) for Light vs. Dark themes.
  4. Payment Processing: Creating families of objects (Validator, Processor, Logger) for different payment providers.
  5. Cloud Resource Provisioning: Creating families of resources (Compute, Storage, Network) for AWS vs. GCP vs. Azure.
  6. Document Generators: Creating families of elements (Header, Footer, Body) for PDF vs. HTML vs. Markdown export.
  7. Game Asset Loading: Creating families of assets (Sprites, Sounds, Physics) for High-Res vs. Low-Res modes.
  8. Testing Environments: Creating families of mocks/stubs for Unit Tests vs. Integration Tests.
  9. FileSystem Abstractions: Creating families of file operations for Local Disk vs. Cloud Storage vs. Memory.
  10. Report Families: Creating families of sections (Summary, Detail, Footer) for different report types (Financial, Operational).

Builder​

Constructs complex objects step by step. Allows you to produce different types and representations of an object using the same construction code.

Problem​

Imagine a complex object that requires laborious, step-by-step initialization of many fields and nested objects. Such initialization code is usually buried inside a monstrous constructor with lots of parameters. Or even worse: scattered all over the client code.

For example, let's think about how to create a House object. To build a simple house, you need to construct four walls and a floor, insert a door and modify the roof. But what if you want a bigger, brighter house, with a backyard and other goodies (like a heating system, plumbing, and electrical wiring)?

The simplest solution is to extend the base House class and create a set of subclasses to cover all combinations of the parameters. But eventually, you'll end up with a huge number of subclasses.

Solution​

The Builder pattern suggests that you extract the object construction code out of its own class and move it to separate objects called builders.

The pattern organizes object construction into a set of steps (buildWalls, buildDoor, etc.). To create an object, you execute a series of these steps on a builder object. The important part is that you don't need to call all of the steps. You can call only those steps that are necessary for producing a particular configuration of an object.

Structure​

How to Implement​

  1. Make sure that you can clearly define the common construction steps for building all available product representations. Otherwise, you won't be able to proceed with implementing the pattern.
  2. Declare these steps in the base builder interface.
  3. Create a concrete builder class for each of the product representations and implement their construction steps. Don't forget to implement a method for fetching the result of the construction.
  4. Think about creating a director class. It may encapsulate various ways to construct a product using the same builder object.
  5. The client code creates both the builder and the director objects. Before construction starts, the client must pass a builder object to the director. Usually, the client does this only once, via parameters of the director's constructor. The director uses the builder object in all further construction.

TypeScript Example​

class Product {
  public parts: string[] = [];
}

interface Builder {
  producePartA(): void;
  producePartB(): void;
  producePartC(): void;
}

class ConcreteBuilder implements Builder {
  private product: Product;

  constructor() {
    this.reset();
  }

  public reset(): void {
    this.product = new Product();
  }

  public producePartA(): void {
    this.product.parts.push('PartA1');
  }

  public producePartB(): void {
    this.product.parts.push('PartB1');
  }

  public producePartC(): void {
    this.product.parts.push('PartC1');
  }

  public getProduct(): Product {
    const result = this.product;
    this.reset();
    return result;
  }
}

Go Example​

package main

import "fmt"

type Builder interface {
    reset()
    setSeats(int)
    setEngine(string)
    setTripComputer(bool)
    setGPS(bool)
}

type Car struct {
    seats        int
    engine       string
    tripComputer bool
    gps          bool
}

type CarBuilder struct {
    car Car
}

func newCarBuilder() *CarBuilder {
    return &CarBuilder{}
}

func (b *CarBuilder) reset() {
    b.car = Car{}
}

func (b *CarBuilder) setSeats(number int) {
    b.car.seats = number
}

func (b *CarBuilder) setEngine(engine string) {
    b.car.engine = engine
}

func (b *CarBuilder) setTripComputer(hasTripComputer bool) {
    b.car.tripComputer = hasTripComputer
}

func (b *CarBuilder) setGPS(hasGPS bool) {
    b.car.gps = hasGPS
}

func (b *CarBuilder) getResult() Car {
    return b.car
}

Pros and Cons​

ProsCons
✓ You can construct objects step-by-step, defer construction steps or run steps recursively.✗ The overall complexity of the code increases since the pattern requires creating multiple new classes.
✓ You can reuse the same construction code when building various representations of products.
✓ Single Responsibility Principle. You can isolate complex construction code from the business logic of the product.

Relations with Other Patterns​

  • Builder focuses on constructing complex objects step by step. Abstract Factory specializes in creating families of related objects.
  • You can use Builder when creating complex Composite trees because you can program its construction steps to work recursively.
  • You can combine Builder with Bridge: the director class plays the role of the abstraction, while different builders act as implementations.

Real-World Use Cases​

1. HTTP Request Builder​

Building complex HTTP requests with headers, query parameters, and body.

JavaScript Implementation:

class HTTPRequest {
  constructor() {
    this.url = '';
    this.method = 'GET';
    this.headers = {};
    this.params = {};
    this.body = null;
  }
}

class HTTPRequestBuilder {
  constructor() {
    this.request = new HTTPRequest();
  }

  setURL(url) {
    this.request.url = url;
    return this;
  }

  setMethod(method) {
    this.request.method = method;
    return this;
  }

  addHeader(key, value) {
    this.request.headers[key] = value;
    return this;
  }

  addQueryParam(key, value) {
    this.request.params[key] = value;
    return this;
  }

  setBody(body) {
    this.request.body = body;
    return this;
  }

  build() {
    return this.request;
  }

  async execute() {
    const queryString = new URLSearchParams(this.request.params).toString();
    const url = queryString ? `${this.request.url}?${queryString}` : this.request.url;

    const options = {
      method: this.request.method,
      headers: this.request.headers,
    };

    if (this.request.body) {
      options.body = JSON.stringify(this.request.body);
    }

    const response = await fetch(url, options);
    return response.json();
  }
}

// Usage
const request = new HTTPRequestBuilder()
  .setURL('https://api.example.com/users')
  .setMethod('POST')
  .addHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json')
  .addHeader('Authorization', 'Bearer token123')
  .addQueryParam('page', '1')
  .setBody({ name: 'John', email: 'john@example.com' })
  .build();

Go Implementation:

type HTTPRequest struct {
    URL     string
    Method  string
    Headers map[string]string
    Params  map[string]string
    Body    []byte
}

type HTTPRequestBuilder struct {
    request *HTTPRequest
}

func NewHTTPRequestBuilder() *HTTPRequestBuilder {
    return &HTTPRequestBuilder{
        request: &HTTPRequest{
            Method:  "GET",
            Headers: make(map[string]string),
            Params:  make(map[string]string),
        },
    }
}

func (b *HTTPRequestBuilder) SetURL(url string) *HTTPRequestBuilder {
    b.request.URL = url
    return b
}

func (b *HTTPRequestBuilder) SetMethod(method string) *HTTPRequestBuilder {
    b.request.Method = method
    return b
}

func (b *HTTPRequestBuilder) AddHeader(key, value string) *HTTPRequestBuilder {
    b.request.Headers[key] = value
    return b
}

func (b *HTTPRequestBuilder) AddQueryParam(key, value string) *HTTPRequestBuilder {
    b.request.Params[key] = value
    return b
}

func (b *HTTPRequestBuilder) SetBody(body []byte) *HTTPRequestBuilder {
    b.request.Body = body
    return b
}

func (b *HTTPRequestBuilder) Build() *HTTPRequest {
    return b.request
}

// Usage
request := NewHTTPRequestBuilder().
    SetURL("https://api.example.com/users").
    SetMethod("POST").
    AddHeader("Content-Type", "application/json").
    AddQueryParam("page", "1").
    SetBody([]byte(`{"name":"John"}`)).
    Build()

2. SQL Query Builder​

Constructing complex SQL queries programmatically.

JavaScript Implementation:

class SQLQuery {
  constructor() {
    this.selectFields = [];
    this.fromTable = '';
    this.whereConditions = [];
    this.orderByFields = [];
    this.limitValue = null;
    this.offsetValue = null;
  }
}

class SQLQueryBuilder {
  constructor() {
    this.query = new SQLQuery();
  }

  select(...fields) {
    this.query.selectFields.push(...fields);
    return this;
  }

  from(table) {
    this.query.fromTable = table;
    return this;
  }

  where(condition) {
    this.query.whereConditions.push(condition);
    return this;
  }

  orderBy(field, direction = 'ASC') {
    this.query.orderByFields.push(`${field} ${direction}`);
    return this;
  }

  limit(value) {
    this.query.limitValue = value;
    return this;
  }

  offset(value) {
    this.query.offsetValue = value;
    return this;
  }

  build() {
    let sql = `SELECT ${this.query.selectFields.join(', ')}`;
    sql += ` FROM ${this.query.fromTable}`;

    if (this.query.whereConditions.length > 0) {
      sql += ` WHERE ${this.query.whereConditions.join(' AND ')}`;
    }

    if (this.query.orderByFields.length > 0) {
      sql += ` ORDER BY ${this.query.orderByFields.join(', ')}`;
    }

    if (this.query.limitValue) {
      sql += ` LIMIT ${this.query.limitValue}`;
    }

    if (this.query.offsetValue) {
      sql += ` OFFSET ${this.query.offsetValue}`;
    }

    return sql;
  }
}

// Usage
const sql = new SQLQueryBuilder()
  .select('id', 'name', 'email')
  .from('users')
  .where('age > 18')
  .where('status = "active"')
  .orderBy('created_at', 'DESC')
  .limit(10)
  .offset(0)
  .build();

console.log(sql);
// SELECT id, name, email FROM users WHERE age > 18 AND status = "active" ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10 OFFSET 0

Go Implementation:

type SQLQuery struct {
    selectFields    []string
    fromTable       string
    whereConditions []string
    orderByFields   []string
    limitValue      *int
    offsetValue     *int
}

type SQLQueryBuilder struct {
    query *SQLQuery
}

func NewSQLQueryBuilder() *SQLQueryBuilder {
    return &SQLQueryBuilder{
        query: &SQLQuery{
            selectFields:    make([]string, 0),
            whereConditions: make([]string, 0),
            orderByFields:   make([]string, 0),
        },
    }
}

func (b *SQLQueryBuilder) Select(fields ...string) *SQLQueryBuilder {
    b.query.selectFields = append(b.query.selectFields, fields...)
    return b
}

func (b *SQLQueryBuilder) From(table string) *SQLQueryBuilder {
    b.query.fromTable = table
    return b
}

func (b *SQLQueryBuilder) Where(condition string) *SQLQueryBuilder {
    b.query.whereConditions = append(b.query.whereConditions, condition)
    return b
}

func (b *SQLQueryBuilder) OrderBy(field, direction string) *SQLQueryBuilder {
    b.query.orderByFields = append(b.query.orderByFields, field+" "+direction)
    return b
}

func (b *SQLQueryBuilder) Limit(value int) *SQLQueryBuilder {
    b.query.limitValue = &value
    return b
}

func (b *SQLQueryBuilder) Build() string {
    sql := fmt.Sprintf("SELECT %s FROM %s",
        strings.Join(b.query.selectFields, ", "),
        b.query.fromTable)

    if len(b.query.whereConditions) > 0 {
        sql += " WHERE " + strings.Join(b.query.whereConditions, " AND ")
    }

    if len(b.query.orderByFields) > 0 {
        sql += " ORDER BY " + strings.Join(b.query.orderByFields, ", ")
    }

    if b.query.limitValue != nil {
        sql += fmt.Sprintf(" LIMIT %d", *b.query.limitValue)
    }

    return sql
}

// Usage
sql := NewSQLQueryBuilder().
    Select("id", "name", "email").
    From("users").
    Where("age > 18").
    OrderBy("created_at", "DESC").
    Limit(10).
    Build()

3. Email Builder​

Creating complex email messages with attachments, HTML content, and recipients.

JavaScript Implementation:

class Email {
  constructor() {
    this.from = '';
    this.to = [];
    this.cc = [];
    this.bcc = [];
    this.subject = '';
    this.htmlBody = '';
    this.textBody = '';
    this.attachments = [];
  }
}

class EmailBuilder {
  constructor() {
    this.email = new Email();
  }

  setFrom(email, name = '') {
    this.email.from = name ? `${name} <${email}>` : email;
    return this;
  }

  addTo(email, name = '') {
    this.email.to.push(name ? `${name} <${email}>` : email);
    return this;
  }

  addCC(email, name = '') {
    this.email.cc.push(name ? `${name} <${email}>` : email);
    return this;
  }

  addBCC(email, name = '') {
    this.email.bcc.push(name ? `${name} <${email}>` : email);
    return this;
  }

  setSubject(subject) {
    this.email.subject = subject;
    return this;
  }

  setHTMLBody(html) {
    this.email.htmlBody = html;
    return this;
  }

  setTextBody(text) {
    this.email.textBody = text;
    return this;
  }

  addAttachment(filename, content, contentType) {
    this.email.attachments.push({ filename, content, contentType });
    return this;
  }

  build() {
    return this.email;
  }

  async send() {
    console.log('Sending email...');
    console.log(`From: ${this.email.from}`);
    console.log(`To: ${this.email.to.join(', ')}`);
    console.log(`Subject: ${this.email.subject}`);
    // Integrate with email service (SendGrid, Mailgun, etc.)
    return { sent: true, messageId: 'msg_' + Date.now() };
  }
}

// Usage
const email = new EmailBuilder()
  .setFrom('sender@example.com', 'John Doe')
  .addTo('recipient@example.com', 'Jane Smith')
  .addCC('manager@example.com')
  .setSubject('Important Update')
  .setHTMLBody('<h1>Hello</h1><p>This is an important message.</p>')
  .setTextBody('Hello\n\nThis is an important message.')
  .addAttachment('report.pdf', Buffer.from('PDF content'), 'application/pdf')
  .build();

await email.send();

Go Implementation:

type Attachment struct {
    Filename    string
    Content     []byte
    ContentType string
}

type Email struct {
    From        string
    To          []string
    CC          []string
    BCC         []string
    Subject     string
    HTMLBody    string
    TextBody    string
    Attachments []Attachment
}

type EmailBuilder struct {
    email *Email
}

func NewEmailBuilder() *EmailBuilder {
    return &EmailBuilder{
        email: &Email{
            To:          make([]string, 0),
            CC:          make([]string, 0),
            BCC:         make([]string, 0),
            Attachments: make([]Attachment, 0),
        },
    }
}

func (b *EmailBuilder) SetFrom(email, name string) *EmailBuilder {
    if name != "" {
        b.email.From = fmt.Sprintf("%s <%s>", name, email)
    } else {
        b.email.From = email
    }
    return b
}

func (b *EmailBuilder) AddTo(email, name string) *EmailBuilder {
    if name != "" {
        b.email.To = append(b.email.To, fmt.Sprintf("%s <%s>", name, email))
    } else {
        b.email.To = append(b.email.To, email)
    }
    return b
}

func (b *EmailBuilder) SetSubject(subject string) *EmailBuilder {
    b.email.Subject = subject
    return b
}

func (b *EmailBuilder) SetHTMLBody(html string) *EmailBuilder {
    b.email.HTMLBody = html
    return b
}

func (b *EmailBuilder) AddAttachment(filename string, content []byte, contentType string) *EmailBuilder {
    b.email.Attachments = append(b.email.Attachments, Attachment{
        Filename:    filename,
        Content:     content,
        ContentType: contentType,
    })
    return b
}

func (b *EmailBuilder) Build() *Email {
    return b.email
}

// Usage
email := NewEmailBuilder().
    SetFrom("sender@example.com", "John Doe").
    AddTo("recipient@example.com", "Jane Smith").
    SetSubject("Important Update").
    SetHTMLBody("<h1>Hello</h1>").
    AddAttachment("report.pdf", []byte("PDF content"), "application/pdf").
