5. UI Form Builder​

Constructing complex forms with validation rules and field configurations.

JavaScript Implementation:

class FormField {
  constructor(name, type, label) {
    this.name = name;
    this.type = type;
    this.label = label;
    this.required = false;
    this.placeholder = '';
    this.validations = [];
    this.defaultValue = null;
  }
}

class Form {
  constructor() {
    this.fields = [];
    this.submitURL = '';
    this.method = 'POST';
    this.encoding = 'application/json';
  }
}

class FormBuilder {
  constructor() {
    this.form = new Form();
  }

  setSubmitURL(url) {
    this.form.submitURL = url;
    return this;
  }

  setMethod(method) {
    this.form.method = method;
    return this;
  }

  addTextField(name, label) {
    const field = new FormField(name, 'text', label);
    this.form.fields.push(field);
    return new FieldBuilder(this, field);
  }

  addEmailField(name, label) {
    const field = new FormField(name, 'email', label);
    this.form.fields.push(field);
    return new FieldBuilder(this, field);
  }

  addPasswordField(name, label) {
    const field = new FormField(name, 'password', label);
    this.form.fields.push(field);
    return new FieldBuilder(this, field);
  }

  addSelectField(name, label, options) {
    const field = new FormField(name, 'select', label);
    field.options = options;
    this.form.fields.push(field);
    return new FieldBuilder(this, field);
  }

  build() {
    return this.form;
  }
}

class FieldBuilder {
  constructor(formBuilder, field) {
    this.formBuilder = formBuilder;
    this.field = field;
  }

  required() {
    this.field.required = true;
    return this;
  }

  placeholder(text) {
    this.field.placeholder = text;
    return this;
  }

  minLength(length) {
    this.field.validations.push({ type: 'minLength', value: length });
    return this;
  }

  maxLength(length) {
    this.field.validations.push({ type: 'maxLength', value: length });
    return this;
  }

  pattern(regex) {
    this.field.validations.push({ type: 'pattern', value: regex });
    return this;
  }

  defaultValue(value) {
    this.field.defaultValue = value;
    return this;
  }

  and() {
    return this.formBuilder;
  }
}

// Usage
const form = new FormBuilder()
  .setSubmitURL('/api/register')
  .setMethod('POST')
  .addTextField('username', 'Username')
  .required()
  .minLength(3)
  .maxLength(20)
  .placeholder('Enter username')
  .and()
  .addEmailField('email', 'Email Address')
  .required()
  .placeholder('your@email.com')
  .and()
  .addPasswordField('password', 'Password')
  .required()
  .minLength(8)
  .pattern(/^(?=.*[A-Za-z])(?=.*\d)[A-Za-z\d]{8,}$/)
  .and()
  .addSelectField('country', 'Country', ['USA', 'UK', 'Canada'])
  .required()
  .and()
  .build();

console.log(JSON.stringify(form, null, 2));

Go Implementation:

type Validation struct {
    Type  string
    Value interface{}
}

type FormField struct {
    Name         string
    Type         string
    Label        string
    Required     bool
    Placeholder  string
    Validations  []Validation
    DefaultValue interface{}
    Options      []string
}

type Form struct {
    Fields    []FormField
    SubmitURL string
    Method    string
    Encoding  string
}

type FormBuilder struct {
    form *Form
}

func NewFormBuilder() *FormBuilder {
    return &FormBuilder{
        form: &Form{
            Fields:   make([]FormField, 0),
            Method:   "POST",
            Encoding: "application/json",
        },
    }
}

func (b *FormBuilder) SetSubmitURL(url string) *FormBuilder {
    b.form.SubmitURL = url
    return b
}

func (b *FormBuilder) AddTextField(name, label string) *FieldBuilder {
    field := FormField{
        Name:        name,
        Type:        "text",
        Label:       label,
        Validations: make([]Validation, 0),
    }
    b.form.Fields = append(b.form.Fields, field)
    return &FieldBuilder{
        formBuilder: b,
        field:       &b.form.Fields[len(b.form.Fields)-1],
    }
}

func (b *FormBuilder) Build() *Form {
    return b.form
}

type FieldBuilder struct {
    formBuilder *FormBuilder
    field       *FormField
}

func (fb *FieldBuilder) Required() *FieldBuilder {
    fb.field.Required = true
    return fb
}

func (fb *FieldBuilder) Placeholder(text string) *FieldBuilder {
    fb.field.Placeholder = text
    return fb
}

func (fb *FieldBuilder) MinLength(length int) *FieldBuilder {
    fb.field.Validations = append(fb.field.Validations, Validation{
        Type:  "minLength",
        Value: length,
    })
    return fb
}

func (fb *FieldBuilder) And() *FormBuilder {
    return fb.formBuilder
}

// Usage
form := NewFormBuilder().
    SetSubmitURL("/api/register").
    AddTextField("username", "Username").
        Required().
        MinLength(3).
        Placeholder("Enter username").
        And().
    Build()

6. Configuration Builder​

Building application configuration with environment-specific settings.

JavaScript Implementation:

class AppConfig {
  constructor() {
    this.database = {};
    this.server = {};
    this.logging = {};
    this.cache = {};
    this.features = {};
  }
}

class ConfigBuilder {
  constructor(environment = 'development') {
    this.config = new AppConfig();
    this.environment = environment;
  }

  setDatabase(config) {
    this.config.database = { ...this.config.database, ...config };
    return this;
  }

  setServer(config) {
    this.config.server = { ...this.config.server, ...config };
    return this;
  }

  setLogging(config) {
    this.config.logging = { ...this.config.logging, ...config };
    return this;
  }

  setCache(config) {
    this.config.cache = { ...this.config.cache, ...config };
    return this;
  }

  enableFeature(featureName) {
    this.config.features[featureName] = true;
    return this;
  }

  disableFeature(featureName) {
    this.config.features[featureName] = false;
    return this;
  }

  loadFromEnv() {
    if (process.env.DATABASE_URL) {
      this.setDatabase({ url: process.env.DATABASE_URL });
    }
    if (process.env.PORT) {
      this.setServer({ port: parseInt(process.env.PORT) });
    }
    return this;
  }

  build() {
    // Apply environment-specific defaults
    if (this.environment === 'production') {
      this.config.logging.level = this.config.logging.level || 'error';
      this.config.server.port = this.config.server.port || 80;
    } else {
      this.config.logging.level = this.config.logging.level || 'debug';
      this.config.server.port = this.config.server.port || 3000;
    }

    return this.config;
  }
}

// Usage
const config = new ConfigBuilder('production')
  .setDatabase({
    host: 'localhost',
    port: 5432,
    name: 'myapp',
    pool: { min: 2, max: 10 },
  })
  .setServer({
    port: 8080,
    host: '0.0.0.0',
    cors: true,
  })
  .setLogging({
    level: 'info',
    format: 'json',
    destination: '/var/log/app.log',
  })
  .setCache({
    enabled: true,
    ttl: 3600,
    provider: 'redis',
  })
  .enableFeature('newUI')
  .enableFeature('analytics')
  .disableFeature('betaFeatures')
  .loadFromEnv()
  .build();

Go Implementation:

type DatabaseConfig struct {
    Host string
    Port int
    Name string
}

type ServerConfig struct {
    Port int
    Host string
    CORS bool
}

type LoggingConfig struct {
    Level       string
    Format      string
    Destination string
}

type AppConfig struct {
    Database DatabaseConfig
    Server   ServerConfig
    Logging  LoggingConfig
    Features map[string]bool
}

type ConfigBuilder struct {
    config      *AppConfig
    environment string
}

func NewConfigBuilder(environment string) *ConfigBuilder {
    return &ConfigBuilder{
        config: &AppConfig{
            Features: make(map[string]bool),
        },
        environment: environment,
    }
}

func (b *ConfigBuilder) SetDatabase(host string, port int, name string) *ConfigBuilder {
    b.config.Database = DatabaseConfig{
        Host: host,
        Port: port,
        Name: name,
    }
    return b
}

func (b *ConfigBuilder) SetServer(host string, port int, cors bool) *ConfigBuilder {
    b.config.Server = ServerConfig{
        Host: host,
        Port: port,
        CORS: cors,
    }
    return b
}

func (b *ConfigBuilder) SetLogging(level, format, destination string) *ConfigBuilder {
    b.config.Logging = LoggingConfig{
        Level:       level,
        Format:      format,
        Destination: destination,
    }
    return b
}

func (b *ConfigBuilder) EnableFeature(featureName string) *ConfigBuilder {
    b.config.Features[featureName] = true
    return b
}

func (b *ConfigBuilder) Build() *AppConfig {
    // Apply environment-specific defaults
    if b.environment == "production" {
        if b.config.Logging.Level == "" {
            b.config.Logging.Level = "error"
        }
        if b.config.Server.Port == 0 {
            b.config.Server.Port = 80
        }
    } else {
        if b.config.Logging.Level == "" {
            b.config.Logging.Level = "debug"
        }
        if b.config.Server.Port == 0 {
            b.config.Server.Port = 3000
        }
    }

    return b.config
}

// Usage
config := NewConfigBuilder("production").
    SetDatabase("localhost", 5432, "myapp").
    SetServer("0.0.0.0", 8080, true).
    SetLogging("info", "json", "/var/log/app.log").
    EnableFeature("newUI").
    Build()

Creating complex test fixtures with realistic data.

JavaScript Implementation:

class User {
  constructor() {
    this.id = null;
    this.username = '';
    this.email = '';
    this.profile = {};
    this.preferences = {};
    this.createdAt = new Date();
  }
}

class UserBuilder {
  constructor() {
    this.user = new User();
    this.user.id = Math.floor(Math.random() * 10000);
  }

  withUsername(username) {
    this.user.username = username;
    return this;
  }

  withEmail(email) {
    this.user.email = email;
    return this;
  }

  withProfile(profile) {
    this.user.profile = { ...this.user.profile, ...profile };
    return this;
  }

  withAge(age) {
    this.user.profile.age = age;
    return this;
  }

  withLocation(city, country) {
    this.user.profile.location = { city, country };
    return this;
  }

  withPreference(key, value) {
    this.user.preferences[key] = value;
    return this;
  }

  createdDaysAgo(days) {
    const date = new Date();
    date.setDate(date.getDate() - days);
    this.user.createdAt = date;
    return this;
  }

  build() {
    // Set defaults if not provided
    if (!this.user.username) {
      this.user.username = `user_${this.user.id}`;
    }
    if (!this.user.email) {
      this.user.email = `${this.user.username}@example.com`;
    }
    return this.user;
  }
}

// Usage in tests
describe('User Service', () => {
  it('should create a premium user', () => {
    const user = new UserBuilder()
      .withUsername('john_doe')
      .withEmail('john@example.com')
      .withAge(30)

      .withPreference('theme', 'dark')
      .withPreference('notifications', true)
      .createdDaysAgo(30)
      .build();

    expect(user.username).toBe('john_doe');
    expect(user.profile.age).toBe(30);
  });
});

Go Implementation:

type Profile struct {
    Age      int
    Location map[string]string
}

type User struct {
    ID          int
    Username    string
    Email       string
    Profile     Profile
    Preferences map[string]interface{}
    CreatedAt   time.Time
}

type UserBuilder struct {
    user *User
}

func NewUserBuilder() *UserBuilder {
    return &UserBuilder{
        user: &User{
            ID:          rand.Intn(10000),
            Preferences: make(map[string]interface{}),
            CreatedAt:   time.Now(),
        },
    }
}

func (b *UserBuilder) WithUsername(username string) *UserBuilder {
    b.user.Username = username
    return b
}

func (b *UserBuilder) WithEmail(email string) *UserBuilder {
    b.user.Email = email
    return b
}

func (b *UserBuilder) WithAge(age int) *UserBuilder {
    b.user.Profile.Age = age
    return b
}

func (b *UserBuilder) WithLocation(city, country string) *UserBuilder {

        "city":    city,
        "country": country,
    }
    return b
}

func (b *UserBuilder) WithPreference(key string, value interface{}) *UserBuilder {
    b.user.Preferences[key] = value
    return b
}

func (b *UserBuilder) CreatedDaysAgo(days int) *UserBuilder {
    b.user.CreatedAt = time.Now().AddDate(0, 0, -days)

}

func (b *UserBuilder) Build() *User {

    }
    if b.user.Email == "" {

    }
    return b.user
}

8. GraphQL Query Builder​

Constructing complex GraphQL queries programmatically.

JavaScript Implementation:

class GraphQLQuery {
  constructor() {
    this.operation = 'query';
    this.name = '';
    this.fields = [];
    this.variables = {};
    this.fragments = [];
  }
}

class GraphQLQueryBuilder {
  constructor(operationType = 'query') {
    this.query = new GraphQLQuery();
    this.query.operation = operationType;
  }

  named(name) {
    this.query.name = name;
    return this;
  }

  addField(field, subFields = null) {
    if (subFields) {
      this.query.fields.push({ name: field, subFields });
    } else {
      this.query.fields.push(field);
    }
    return this;
  }

  addVariable(name, type, defaultValue = null) {
    this.query.variables[name] = { type, defaultValue };
    return this;
  }

  build() {
    let queryString = this.query.operation;

    if (this.query.name) {
      queryString += ` ${this.query.name}`;
    }

    // Add variables
    if (Object.keys(this.query.variables).length > 0) {
      const vars = Object.entries(this.query.variables)
        .map(([name, { type }]) => `$${name}: ${type}`)
        .join(', ');
      queryString += `(${vars})`;
    }

    // Add fields
    queryString += ' {\n';
    this.query.fields.forEach((field) => {
      if (typeof field === 'string') {
        queryString += `  ${field}\n`;
      } else {
        queryString += `  ${field.name} {\n`;
        field.subFields.forEach((sf) => {
          queryString += `    ${sf}\n`;
        });
        queryString += `  }\n`;
      }
    });
    queryString += '}';

    return queryString;
  }
}

// Usage
const query = new GraphQLQueryBuilder('query')
  .named('GetUser')
  .addVariable('id', 'ID!')
  .addField('user(id: $id)', ['id', 'username', 'email', 'profile { age location }'])
  .build();

console.log(query);
/*
query GetUser($id: ID!) {
  user(id: $id) {
    id
    username
    email
    profile { age location }
  }
}
*/

Go Implementation:

type GraphQLField struct {
    Name      string
    SubFields []string
}

type GraphQLQuery struct {
    Operation string
    Name      string
    Fields    []interface{}
    Variables map[string]string
}

type GraphQLQueryBuilder struct {
    query *GraphQLQuery
}

func NewGraphQLQueryBuilder(operationType string) *GraphQLQueryBuilder {
    return &GraphQLQueryBuilder{
        query: &GraphQLQuery{
            Operation: operationType,
            Fields:    make([]interface{}, 0),
            Variables: make(map[string]string),
        },
    }
}

func (b *GraphQLQueryBuilder) Named(name string) *GraphQLQueryBuilder {
    b.query.Name = name
    return b
}

func (b *GraphQLQueryBuilder) AddField(field string, subFields []string) *GraphQLQueryBuilder {
    if subFields != nil {
        b.query.Fields = append(b.query.Fields, GraphQLField{
            Name:      field,
            SubFields: subFields,
        })
    } else {
        b.query.Fields = append(b.query.Fields, field)
    }
    return b
}

func (b *GraphQLQueryBuilder) AddVariable(name, varType string) *GraphQLQueryBuilder {
    b.query.Variables[name] = varType
    return b
}

func (b *GraphQLQueryBuilder) Build() string {
    queryString := b.query.Operation

    if b.query.Name != "" {
        queryString += " " + b.query.Name
    }

    // Add variables
    if len(b.query.Variables) > 0 {
        vars := make([]string, 0)
        for name, varType := range b.query.Variables {
            vars = append(vars, fmt.Sprintf("$%s: %s", name, varType))
        }
        queryString += fmt.Sprintf("(%s)", strings.Join(vars, ", "))
    }

    // Add fields
    queryString += " {\n"
    for _, field := range b.query.Fields {
        switch f := field.(type) {
        case string:
            queryString += fmt.Sprintf("  %s\n", f)
        case GraphQLField:
            queryString += fmt.Sprintf("  %s {\n", f.Name)
            for _, sf := range f.SubFields {
                queryString += fmt.Sprintf("    %s\n", sf)
            }
            queryString += "  }\n"
        }
    }
    queryString += "}"

    return queryString
}

// Usage
query := NewGraphQLQueryBuilder("query").
    Named("GetUser").
    AddVariable("id", "ID!").
    AddField("user(id: $id)", []string{"id", "username", "email"}).
    Build()

9. Pipeline Builder​

Creating data processing pipelines with multiple stages.

JavaScript Implementation:

class Pipeline {
  constructor() {
    this.stages = [];
    this.errorHandlers = [];
  }
}

class PipelineBuilder {
  constructor() {
    this.pipeline = new Pipeline();
  }

  addStage(name, processor) {
    this.pipeline.stages.push({ name, processor });
    return this;
  }

  addFilter(name, predicate) {
    this.pipeline.stages.push({
      name,
      processor: (data) => data.filter(predicate),
    });
    return this;
  }

  addMap(name, mapper) {
    this.pipeline.stages.push({
      name,
      processor: (data) => data.map(mapper),
    });
    return this;
  }

  addReduce(name, reducer, initialValue) {
    this.pipeline.stages.push({
      name,
      processor: (data) => data.reduce(reducer, initialValue),
    });
    return this;
  }

  onError(handler) {
    this.pipeline.errorHandlers.push(handler);
    return this;
  }

  build() {
    return async (initialData) => {
      let data = initialData;

      for (const stage of this.pipeline.stages) {
        try {
          console.log(`Executing stage: ${stage.name}`);
          data = await stage.processor(data);
        } catch (error) {
          console.error(`Error in stage ${stage.name}:`, error);

          for (const handler of this.pipeline.errorHandlers) {
            handler(error, stage.name);
          }

          throw error;
        }
      }

      return data;
    };
  }
}

// Usage
const dataPipeline = new PipelineBuilder()
  .addStage('validate', (data) => {
    return data.filter((item) => item.id && item.value);
  })
  .addMap('transform', (item) => ({
    ...item,
    value: item.value * 2,
    timestamp: Date.now(),
  }))
  .addFilter('filter-positive', (item) => item.value > 0)
  .addReduce(
    'aggregate',
    (acc, item) => {
      acc.total += item.value;
      acc.count += 1;
      return acc;
    },
    { total: 0, count: 0 },
  )
  .onError((error, stageName) => {
    console.log(`Logging error from ${stageName} to monitoring service`);
  })
  .build();

// Execute pipeline
const inputData = [
  { id: 1, value: 10 },
  { id: 2, value: 20 },
  { id: 3, value: -5 },
];

const result = await dataPipeline(inputData);
console.log(result); // { total: 60, count: 2 }

Go Implementation:

type Stage struct {
    Name      string
    Processor func(interface{}) (interface{}, error)
}

type Pipeline struct {
    Stages        []Stage
    ErrorHandlers []func(error, string)
}

type PipelineBuilder struct {
    pipeline *Pipeline
}

func NewPipelineBuilder() *PipelineBuilder {
    return &PipelineBuilder{
        pipeline: &Pipeline{
            Stages:        make([]Stage, 0),
            ErrorHandlers: make([]func(error, string), 0),
        },
    }
}

func (b *PipelineBuilder) AddStage(name string, processor func(interface{}) (interface{}, error)) *PipelineBuilder {
    b.pipeline.Stages = append(b.pipeline.Stages, Stage{
        Name:      name,
        Processor: processor,
    })
    return b
}

func (b *PipelineBuilder) OnError(handler func(error, string)) *PipelineBuilder {
    b.pipeline.ErrorHandlers = append(b.pipeline.ErrorHandlers, handler)
    return b
}

func (b *PipelineBuilder) Build() func(interface{}) (interface{}, error) {
    return func(initialData interface{}) (interface{}, error) {
        data := initialData

        for _, stage := range b.pipeline.Stages {
            fmt.Printf("Executing stage: %s\n", stage.Name)

            result, err := stage.Processor(data)
            if err != nil {
                fmt.Printf("Error in stage %s: %v\n", stage.Name, err)

                for _, handler := range b.pipeline.ErrorHandlers {
                    handler(err, stage.Name)
                }

                return nil, err
            }

            data = result
        }

        return data, nil
    }
}

// Usage
pipeline := NewPipelineBuilder().
    AddStage("validate", func(data interface{}) (interface{}, error) {
        // Validation logic
        return data, nil
    }).
    AddStage("transform", func(data interface{}) (interface{}, error) {
        // Transformation logic
        return data, nil
    }).
    OnError(func(err error, stageName string) {
        fmt.Printf("Logging error from %s\n", stageName)
    }).
    Build()

result, err := pipeline(inputData)

10. REST API Client Builder​

Building configurable HTTP API clients with interceptors and retry logic.

JavaScript Implementation:

class APIClient {
  constructor() {
    this.baseURL = '';
    this.headers = {};
    this.timeout = 30000;
    this.retries = 0;
    this.retryDelay = 1000;
    this.interceptors = {
      request: [],
      response: [],
    };
  }
}

class APIClientBuilder {
  constructor() {
    this.client = new APIClient();
  }

  setBaseURL(url) {
    this.client.baseURL = url;
    return this;
  }

  addHeader(key, value) {
    this.client.headers[key] = value;
    return this;
  }

  setAuth(token, type = 'Bearer') {
    this.client.headers['Authorization'] = `${type} ${token}`;
    return this;
  }

  setTimeout(ms) {
    this.client.timeout = ms;
    return this;
  }

  setRetries(count, delay = 1000) {
    this.client.retries = count;
    this.client.retryDelay = delay;
    return this;
  }

  addRequestInterceptor(interceptor) {
    this.client.interceptors.request.push(interceptor);
    return this;
  }

  addResponseInterceptor(interceptor) {
    this.client.interceptors.response.push(interceptor);
    return this;
  }

  build() {
    const client = this.client;

    return {
      async request(method, endpoint, data = null) {
        let config = {
          method,
          url: `${client.baseURL}${endpoint}`,
          headers: { ...client.headers },
          timeout: client.timeout,
        };

        if (data) {
          config.body = JSON.stringify(data);
        }

        // Apply request interceptors
        for (const interceptor of client.interceptors.request) {
          config = await interceptor(config);
        }

        // Retry logic
        let lastError;
        for (let attempt = 0; attempt <= client.retries; attempt++) {
          try {
            let response = await fetch(config.url, config);
            let responseData = await response.json();

            // Apply response interceptors
            for (const interceptor of client.interceptors.response) {
              responseData = await interceptor(responseData);
            }

            return responseData;
          } catch (error) {
            lastError = error;
            if (attempt < client.retries) {
              await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, client.retryDelay));
            }
          }
        }

        throw lastError;
      },

      get(endpoint) {
        return this.request('GET', endpoint);
      },

      post(endpoint, data) {
        return this.request('POST', endpoint, data);
      },

      put(endpoint, data) {
        return this.request('PUT', endpoint, data);
      },

      delete(endpoint) {
        return this.request('DELETE', endpoint);
      },
    };
  }
}

// Usage
const apiClient = new APIClientBuilder()
  .setBaseURL('https://api.example.com')
  .addHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json')
  .setAuth('my-token-123')
  .setTimeout(5000)
  .setRetries(3, 2000)
  .addRequestInterceptor(async (config) => {
    console.log('Request:', config.method, config.url);
    return config;
  })
  .addResponseInterceptor(async (response) => {
    console.log('Response received');
    return response;
  })
  .build();

// Use the client
const users = await apiClient.get('/users');
const newUser = await apiClient.post('/users', {
  name: 'John Doe',
  email: 'john@example.com',
});

Go Implementation:

type RequestInterceptor func(*http.Request) (*http.Request, error)
type ResponseInterceptor func(*http.Response) (*http.Response, error)

type APIClient struct {
    BaseURL             string
    Headers             map[string]string
    Timeout             time.Duration
    Retries             int
    RetryDelay          time.Duration
    RequestInterceptors []RequestInterceptor
    ResponseInterceptors []ResponseInterceptor
    Client              *http.Client
}

type APIClientBuilder struct {
    client *APIClient
}

func NewAPIClientBuilder() *APIClientBuilder {
    return &APIClientBuilder{
        client: &APIClient{
            Headers:             make(map[string]string),
            Timeout:             30 * time.Second,
            Retries:             0,
            RetryDelay:          1 * time.Second,
            RequestInterceptors: make([]RequestInterceptor, 0),
            ResponseInterceptors: make([]ResponseInterceptor, 0),
        },
    }
}

func (b *APIClientBuilder) SetBaseURL(url string) *APIClientBuilder {
    b.client.BaseURL = url
    return b
}

func (b *APIClientBuilder) AddHeader(key, value string) *APIClientBuilder {
    b.client.Headers[key] = value
    return b
}

func (b *APIClientBuilder) SetAuth(token, authType string) *APIClientBuilder {
    b.client.Headers["Authorization"] = fmt.Sprintf("%s %s", authType, token)
    return b
}

func (b *APIClientBuilder) SetTimeout(duration time.Duration) *APIClientBuilder {
    b.client.Timeout = duration
    return b
}

func (b *APIClientBuilder) SetRetries(count int, delay time.Duration) *APIClientBuilder {
    b.client.Retries = count
    b.client.RetryDelay = delay
    return b
}

func (b *APIClientBuilder) AddRequestInterceptor(interceptor RequestInterceptor) *APIClientBuilder {
    b.client.RequestInterceptors = append(b.client.RequestInterceptors, interceptor)
    return b
}

func (b *APIClientBuilder) Build() *APIClient {
    b.client.Client = &http.Client{
        Timeout: b.client.Timeout,
    }
    return b.client
}

func (c *APIClient) Get(endpoint string) (*http.Response, error) {
    return c.Request("GET", endpoint, nil)
}

func (c *APIClient) Post(endpoint string, body []byte) (*http.Response, error) {
    return c.Request("POST", endpoint, body)
}

func (c *APIClient) Request(method, endpoint string, body []byte) (*http.Response, error) {
    url := c.BaseURL + endpoint

    var lastErr error
    for attempt := 0; attempt <= c.Retries; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, url, bytes.NewBuffer(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }

        // Set headers
        for key, value := range c.Headers {
            req.Header.Set(key, value)
        }

        // Apply request interceptors
        for _, interceptor := range c.RequestInterceptors {
            req, err = interceptor(req)
            if err != nil {
                return nil, err
            }
        }

        resp, err := c.Client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            lastErr = err
            if attempt < c.Retries {
                time.Sleep(c.RetryDelay)
                continue
            }
        }

        return resp, nil
    }

    return nil, lastErr
}

// Usage
apiClient := NewAPIClientBuilder().
    SetBaseURL("https://api.example.com").
    AddHeader("Content-Type", "application/json").
    SetAuth("my-token-123", "Bearer").
    SetTimeout(5 * time.Second).
    SetRetries(3, 2*time.Second).
    AddRequestInterceptor(func(req *http.Request) (*http.Request, error) {
        fmt.Printf("Request: %s %s\n", req.Method, req.URL)
        return req, nil
    }).
    Build()

resp, err := apiClient.Get("/users")

Real-World Use Cases​

  1. SQL Query Builder: Constructing complex SQL queries dynamically (e.g., .select().where().orderBy()).
  2. HTTP Request Builder: Building complex API requests with custom headers, body, query params, and timeouts.
  3. DOM Element Construction: Creating complex HTML structures via JavaScript with multiple attributes and children.
  4. Email Composition: Building emails with subject, body, multiple attachments, and varying recipients.
  5. Configuration Objects: Building complex configuration objects with sensible defaults and optional overrides.
  6. Unit Test Fixtures: Setting up complex test data or mock objects step-by-step.
  7. Document Generation: Building PDF or Word documents by appending paragraphs, images, and tables sequentially.
  8. Menu Generation: Constructing nested menu structures with permissions and visibility rules.
  9. Graph/Chart Construction: Building complex data visualization configurations (axes, legends, series).
  10. Pizza/Order Customization: Building custom user orders with many toppings, crusts, and sizes (classic example).

Prototype​

Specifies the kind of objects to create using a prototypical instance, and create new objects by copying this prototype.

Problem​

Say you have an object, and you want to create an exact copy of it. How would you do it? First, you have to create a new object of the same class. Then you have to go through all the fields of the original object and copy their values over to the new object.

Nice and easy, right? Not really. Firstly, not all objects can be copied that way because some of the object's fields may be private and not visible from outside of the object itself.

Secondly, you have to know the object's class to create a duplicate. So your code becomes dependent on that class.

Solution​

The Prototype pattern delegates the cloning process to the actual objects that are being cloned. The pattern declares a common interface for all objects that support cloning. This interface lets you clone an object without coupling your code to the class of that object. Usually, such an interface contains just a single clone method.

Structure​

How to Implement​

  1. Create the prototype interface and declare the clone method in it. Or just add the method to all classes of an existing class hierarchy, if you have one.
  2. A prototype class must define an alternative constructor that accepts an object of that class as an argument. The constructor must copy the values of all fields defined in the class from the passed object into the newly created instance. If you're changing a subclass, you must call the parent constructor to let the superclass handle the cloning of its private fields.
  3. The cloning method usually consists of just one line: running a new operator with the prototypical version of the constructor. Note that every class must explicitly override the cloning method and use its own class name along with the new operator. Otherwise, the cloning method may produce an object of a parent class.

TypeScript Example​

class ComponentWithBackReference {
  public prototype;

  constructor(prototype: Prototype) {
    this.prototype = prototype;
  }
}

class Prototype {
  public primitive: any;
  public component: object;
  public circularReference: ComponentWithBackReference;

  public clone(): this {
    const clone = Object.create(this);

    clone.component = Object.create(this.component);

    // Cloning an object that has a nested object with backreference
    clone.circularReference = {
      ...this.circularReference,
      prototype: { ...this },
    };

    return clone;
  }
}

Go Example​

package main

import "fmt"

type Inode interface {
    print(string)
    clone() Inode
}

type File struct {
    name string
}

func (f *File) print(indentation string) {
    fmt.Println(indentation + f.name)
}

func (f *File) clone() Inode {
    return &File{name: f.name + "_clone"}
}

type Folder struct {
    children []Inode
    name     string
}

func (f *Folder) print(indentation string) {
    fmt.Println(indentation + f.name)
    for _, i := range f.children {
        i.print(indentation + indentation)
    }
}

func (f *Folder) clone() Inode {
    cloneFolder := &Folder{name: f.name + "_clone"}
    var tempChildren []Inode
    for _, i := range f.children {
        copy := i.clone()
        tempChildren = append(tempChildren, copy)
    }
    cloneFolder.children = tempChildren
    return cloneFolder
}

func main() {
    file1 := &File{name: "File1"}
    file2 := &File{name: "File2"}
    file3 := &File{name: "File3"}

    folder1 := &Folder{
        children: []Inode{file1},
        name:     "Folder1",
    }

    folder2 := &Folder{
        children: []Inode{folder1, file2, file3},
        name:     "Folder2",
    }

    fmt.Println("\nPrinting hierarchy for Folder2")
    folder2.print("  ")

    cloneFolder := folder2.clone()
    fmt.Println("\nPrinting hierarchy for clone Folder")
    cloneFolder.print("  ")
}

Pros and Cons​

ProsCons
✓ You can clone objects without coupling to their concrete classes.✗ Cloning complex objects that have circular references might be very tricky.
✓ You can get rid of repeated initialization code in favor of cloning pre-built prototypes.
✓ You can produce complex objects more conveniently.
✓ You get an alternative to inheritance when dealing with configuration presets for complex objects.

Relations with Other Patterns​

  • Many designs start by using Factory Method (less complicated and more customizable via subclasses) and evolve toward Abstract Factory, Prototype, or Builder (more flexible, but more complicated).
  • Abstract Factory classes are often based on a set of Factory Methods, but you can also use Prototype to compose the methods on these classes.
  • Prototype can help when you need to save copies of Commands into history.
  • Designs that make heavy use of Composite and Decorator can often benefit from using Prototype. Cloning a complex structure is easier than reconstructing it from scratch.

Real-World Use Cases​

  1. Object Caching: Storing expensive-to-create objects in a cache and cloning them when needed (e.g., DB connections).
  2. Configuration Defaults: Cloning a default configuration object and modifying specific fields for new environments.
  3. Game Entities: Spawning multiple enemies or NPCs by cloning a base template instance.
  4. UI Component Instantiation: Creating complex UI widgets by cloning a pre-configured template widget.
  5. Document Versioning: Creating a new version of a document by cloning the previous state.
  6. Genetic Algorithms: Creating subsequent generations by cloning and mutating members of the population.
  7. Undo/Redo Operations: Saving state snapshots by cloning the application state object.
  8. Database Record Duplication: Cloning a database record to create a new entry with similar data.
  9. Network Packet Construction: Cloning a template packet and modifying header fields for transmission.
  10. Form Pre-filling: Cloning a previous submission to pre-fill a new form for the user.

Simple Factory​

A simple factory is a function or method that encapsulates object creation logic, often using a switch statement or conditional logic to instantiate different classes based on input parameters. Unlike the Factory Method pattern, it doesn't rely on inheritance or subclasses to decide which object to create.

Problem​

A client code needs to create objects of various classes that share a common interface or parent class. If the client code instantiates these classes directly, it becomes tightly coupled to those concrete classes. Any change in the creation logic or adding a new class requires modifying all client code locations.

Solution​

The Simple Factory suggests moving the instantiation logic to a separate class or a static method. This method takes some input (like a type string or a configuration object) and returns an instance of the appropriate class. The client code only interacts with the factory and the common interface.

Structure​

How to Implement​

  1. Identify the classes that should be created by the factory and ensure they follow a common interface.
  2. Create a factory class or a static method in an existing class.
  3. Implement a decision logic (usually a switch or if-else) that chooses which class to instantiate based on input parameters.
  4. Update the client code to use the factory instead of calling constructors directly.

TypeScript Example​

interface Door {
    getWidth(): number;
    getHeight(): number;
}

class WoodenDoor implements Door {
    constructor(private width: number, private height: number) { }

    public getWidth(): number {
        return this.width;
    }

    public getHeight(): number {
        return this.height;
    }
}

class DoorFactory {
    public static makeDoor(width: number, height: number): Door {
        return new WoodenDoor(width, height);
    }
}

// Usage
const door = DoorFactory.makeDoor(100, 200);
console.log(`Door: ${door.getWidth()}x${door.getHeight()}`);

Go Example​

package main

import "fmt"

type Door interface {
    GetWidth() float32
    GetHeight() float32
}

type WoodenDoor struct {
    width  float32
    height float32
}

func (w *WoodenDoor) GetWidth() float32 {
    return w.width
}

func (w *WoodenDoor) GetHeight() float32 {
    return w.height
}

// Simple Factory function
func MakeDoor(width float32, height float32) Door {
    return &WoodenDoor{
        width:  width,
        height: height,
    }
}

func main() {
    door := MakeDoor(100, 200)
    fmt.Printf("Door: %.2fx%.2f\n", door.GetWidth(), door.GetHeight())
}

Pros and Cons​

ProsCons
✓ Decouples the client code from concrete classes.✗ The factory class can become a "God Object" if too many classes are added.
✓ Consolidation of creation logic in one place simplifies maintenance.✗ Adding new products requires modifying the factory code, violating the Open/Closed Principle.
✓ Makes the client code cleaner and more readable.

Relations with Other Patterns​

  • Simple Factory is often a simplified version of Factory Method. If you find the factory method's inheritance hierarchy too complex, you can collapse it into a single simple factory.
  • Simple Factory can be used as a step in a Facade to provide simplified access to a complex subsystem's components.
  • Unlike Abstract Factory, Simple Factory creates only one product at a time, not families of related objects.

Real-World Use Cases​

  1. Shape Factory: Creating distinct geometric shapes (Circle, Square) based on a type string.
  2. Notification Factory: Instantiating Email, SMS, or Push notifiers based on user preference.
  3. Logger Factory: creating Console, File, or Remote loggers based on environment config.
  4. Payment Processing: creating Stripe, PayPal, or Square processors based on selected method.
  5. User Roles: creating Admin, Editor, or Viewer objects based on login credentials.
  6. Social Media Connector: creating Facebook, Twitter, or LinkedIn connectors based on platform ID.
  7. File Parser: creating JSON, XML, or YAML parsers based on file extension.
  8. Enemy Spawner: creating different enemy types (Goblin, Orc, Troll) based on level difficulty.
  9. Form Elements: creating Input, Select, or Checkbox widgets based on field configuration.
  10. Error Handlers: creating specific error handlers (404, 500) based on HTTP status codes.

Object Pool​

The Object Pool pattern offers a mechanism to reuse objects that are expensive to create. Rather than creating a new instance every time, a pool of initialized objects is maintained. Clients "borrow" objects from the pool and "return" them when done. Used to improve performance in situations where object creation cost is high.

Problem​

Creating certain objects can be a performance bottleneck if they require significant resources, time, or complex initialization (e.g., database connections, large bitmapped objects, or worker threads). Frequent creation and destruction of such objects lead to high memory consumption and garbage collection overhead.

Solution​

The Object Pool pattern suggests creating a pool (a container) that holds a collection of pre-initialized objects. When a client needs an object, it requests one from the pool. After use, instead of destroying the object, the client returns it to the pool for later reuse.

Structure​

How to Implement​

  1. Identify the "Reusable" object and its creation/initialization requirements.
  2. Design an ObjectPool class with lists for keeping track of available and in-use objects.
  3. Implement an acquire method that returns an available object from the pool, creating a new one if the pool is empty (or according to a policy).
  4. Implement a release method that puts the object back into the available list.
  5. Optionally, implement pool size limits, object expiration logic, and thread-safety if needed.

TypeScript Example​

class Reusable {
    public getInstanceId(): number {
        return Math.floor(Math.random() * 10000);
    }
}

class ObjectPool {
    private available: Reusable[] = [];
    private inUse: Reusable[] = [];

    public acquireReusable(): Reusable {
        if (this.available.length === 0) {
            this.available.push(new Reusable());
        }
        const item = this.available.pop()!;
        this.inUse.push(item);
        return item;
    }

    public releaseReusable(item: Reusable): void {
        const index = this.inUse.indexOf(item);
        if (index !== -1) {
            this.inUse.splice(index, 1);
            this.available.push(item);
        }
    }
}

// Usage
const pool = new ObjectPool();
const item1 = pool.acquireReusable();
const item2 = pool.acquireReusable();
console.log('Acquired item 1 ID:', item1.getInstanceId());
console.log('Acquired item 2 ID:', item2.getInstanceId());
pool.releaseReusable(item1);

Go Example​

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "math/rand"
    "sync"
)

type Reusable struct {
    ID int
}

type ObjectPool struct {
    available []*Reusable
    mu        sync.Mutex
}

func (p *ObjectPool) Acquire() *Reusable {
    p.mu.Lock()
    defer p.mu.Unlock()

    if len(p.available) == 0 {
        return &Reusable{ID: rand.Intn(10000)}
    }

    item := p.available[0]
    p.available = p.available[1:]
    return item
}

func (p *ObjectPool) Release(item *Reusable) {
    p.mu.Lock()
    defer p.mu.Unlock()
    p.available = append(p.available, item)
}

func main() {
    pool := &ObjectPool{}
    item1 := pool.Acquire()
    item2 := pool.Acquire()
    
    fmt.Printf("Acquired items with IDs: %d, %d\n", item1.ID, item2.ID)
    
    pool.Release(item1)
    pool.Release(item2)
}

Pros and Cons​

ProsCons
✓ Improves performance by reducing object creation and destruction frequency.✗ Increased management complexity (tracking object states).
✓ Helps manage limited resources by controlling the number of instances.✗ Possibility of object leakage if clients forget to release objects.
✓ Reduces garbage collection overhead.✗ Risk of accessing an object that is in an inconsistent state if it wasn't cleaned properly on release.

Relations with Other Patterns​

  • Object Pool can be used as a source for Factory Method to manage the reuse of created products.
  • Object Pool is often combined with Singleton to ensure there is only one pool manager per resource type and provide global access.
  • Unlike Flyweight, where many clients share a single immutable instance, Object Pool provides mutable instances that are exclusive to one client at a time.

Real-World Use Cases​

  1. Database Connection Pool: reusing active database connections to avoid the handshake overhead.
  2. Thread Pool: reusing a fixed number of worker threads to execute tasks concurrently.
  3. Game Projectiles: reusing bullet/missile objects in games to avoid garbage collection spikes.
  4. Socket Connections: reusing TCP/UDP sockets for network communication.
  5. Graphic Objects: reusing expensive canvas or DOM elements for data visualization.
  6. Audio Buffers: reusing allocated memory buffers for audio processing.
  7. HTTP Clients: reusing HTTP client instances to leverage keep-alive connections.
  8. Large Bitmaps: reusing memory allocated for large image processing operations.
  9. PDF Objects: reusing context objects during mass PDF generation.
  10. Font Objects: reusing loaded font faces in rendering engines.

Lazy Initialization​

Lazy Initialization defers the creation of an object, calculation of a value, or some other expensive process until it is first needed. This contributes to efficiency in the program’s operation and faster startup times.

Problem​

Applications often have resources or objects that are expensive to create, but might not be needed immediately or at all during a specific execution. Initializing all such resources at startup can lead to slow startup times and high initial memory usage.

Solution​

The Lazy Initialization pattern suggests delaying the resource creation until the point of first access. Instead of creating the object in the constructor or at the global scope, we check if the object has already been initialized. If not, we create it and return the instance. All subsequent requests return the cached instance.

Structure​

How to Implement​

  1. Identify the expensive object or resource to be lazily initialized.
  2. Create a wrapper class or a property that will hold the instance.
  3. Implement a getter or a creation method that checks if the instance is null or uninitialized.
  4. If the instance is not initialized, perform the expensive creation and store it.
  5. Return the instance. In multi-threaded environments, ensure that the initialization is thread-safe (e.g., using double-checked locking).

TypeScript Example​

class HeavyProcess {
    constructor() {
        console.log("HeavyProcess initialized (expensive!)");
    }
    
    public process(): void {
        console.log("Processing done.");
    }
}

class LazyWrapper {
    private processInstance: HeavyProcess | null = null;
    
    public get process(): HeavyProcess {
        if (!this.processInstance) {
            this.processInstance = new HeavyProcess();
        }
        return this.processInstance;
    }
}

// Usage
const wrapper = new LazyWrapper();
console.log("Wrapper created, HeavyProcess not untouched yet.");
wrapper.process.process(); // Initialized here
wrapper.process.process(); // Already initialized

Go Example​

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "sync"
)

type HeavyProcess struct {
    data string
}

func NewHeavyProcess() *HeavyProcess {
    fmt.Println("HeavyProcess initialized (expensive!)")
    return &HeavyProcess{data: "heavy data"}
}

type LazyWrapper struct {
    process *HeavyProcess
    once    sync.Once
}

func (l *LazyWrapper) GetProcess() *HeavyProcess {
    l.once.Do(func() {
        l.process = NewHeavyProcess()
    })
    return l.process
}

func main() {
    wrapper := &LazyWrapper{}
    fmt.Println("Wrapper created.")
    
    p1 := wrapper.GetProcess() // Initialized here
    fmt.Println("Data:", p1.data)
    
    p2 := wrapper.GetProcess() // Not initialized again
    fmt.Println("Data:", p2.data)
}

Pros and Cons​

ProsCons
✓ Speeds up the application startup time.✗ Can cause a delay (latency spike) upon the first request to the expensive resource.
✓ Reduces memory footprint by avoiding unnecessary object creation.✗ Increased complexity if thread-safety needs to be managed (potential for race conditions).
✓ Decouples the configuration/startup logic from the resource usage.

Relations with Other Patterns​

  • Singleton often uses Lazy Initialization internally to ensure the instance is created only once when requested.
  • Proxy often uses Lazy Initialization (Virtual Proxy) to delay the initialization of the real object until it's needed.
  • Flyweight uses a factory that typically lazily initializes its shared instances.

Real-World Use Cases​

  1. Heavy UI Components: loading complex widgets (like a rich text editor) only when they become visible.
  2. Database Connection: establishing the actual connection only when the first query is executed.
  3. Config Loading: reading and parsing configuration files only when a config value is requested.
  4. Image Loading: fetching high-resolution images only when they scroll into the viewport (lazy loading).
  5. Plugin System: initializing optional plugins only if they are actually used by the application.
  6. Environment Variables: parsing environment variables or secrets only upon first access.
  7. Singletons: creating the singleton instance only when getInstance is called (Lazy Singleton).
  8. Browser APIs: initializing AudioContext or WebGL context only after user interaction.
  9. External SDKs: initializing Analytics or Ads SDKs only when the first event needs to be tracked.
  10. Translation Data: loading a specific language bundle only when the user switches to that language.
